Groundhog Day was officially celebrated for the first time at Gobbler's Knob in Punxsutawney, Pennsylvania on February 2, 1887. The Punxsutawney Spirit newspaper is credited with printing the news of the first observance in 1886 (one year before the first legendary trek to Gobbler's Knob).

The first official celebration in 1887 was organized by a local newspaper editor named Clymer Freas, who convinced a group of hunters and businessmen called the Punxsutawney Groundhog Club to trek to a spot called Gobbler's Knob.

Phil has been right 39% of the time going back to his first recorded prediction in 1887. The tradition has roots in European customs, particularly German Candlemas Day traditions that were brought to Pennsylvania by German immigrants in the 18th and 19th centuries.

Pope Paul II mediated the Second Peace of Torun (October 19, 1466) in which the Sword Brothers lost half of Prussia outright and accepted Casimir's suzerainty in the rump lands left to them.

This peace treaty concluded the Thirteen Years' War (1454–1466) which had begun in February 1454 with the revolt of the Prussian Confederation, led by the cities of Danzig (Gdańsk), Elbing (Elbląg), Kulm (Chełmno) and Thorn, and the Prussian gentry against the rule of the Teutonic Knights in the Monastic State.

With help from the papal legate, Rudolf of Rüdesheim, the Second Peace of Thorn was signed on 10 October 1466. Western Prussia became an autonomous Polish province, later known as Royal Prussia, and Eastern Prussia remained under the Teutonic Knights, but they became a vassal of the Polish king, meaning they had to swear loyalty to the Polish king. The Grand Master also became a Senator in the Polish kingdom.

results:
Based on the search results, here's what the Pruett rule defines as a blue moon:

The practice of designating the second full moon in a month as "blue" originated with amateur astronomer James Hugh Pruett in 1946. He either misread the Maine almanac's definition or interpreted the meaning of "blue moon" differently, calling it the second full moon in a month.

Pruett's interpretation became widely adopted. Today, Pruett's misinterpreted "two full moons in a month rule" is recognized worldwide. A calendrical blue moon (by Pruett's definition) is predictable and relatively common, happening 7 times in every 19 years (once every 2 or 3 years).

It's worth noting that the original Maine Farmers' Almanac rule had been all but forgotten, which instead defined a blue moon as the third full moon when a season contains four full moons.

In 1851, Robert Campbell from the Hudson's Bay Company became the first white man known to have entered Hän territory, when he traveled from Fort Selkirk to Fort Yukon. However, the Hän had little contact with non-Indigenous peoples until 1847, when fur traders from the Hudson's Bay Company built Fort Yukon not far from their territory.

Following this initial contact, trading posts were set up in 1873 and 1874 (after the United States purchase of Alaska), with one established by Moses Mercier and another, Fort Reliance, established by Alaska Commercial Company traders. Gradually trading with whites resulted in the Hän shifting from their traditional fishing-hunting economy to a fur-trapping economy, as they grew increasingly reliant on European goods such as guns, clothing, and canvas from 1887 to 1895.

The arrival of European settlers, particularly during the Klondike Gold Rush in the late 19th century, significantly disrupted their traditional ways of life.

Here are the search results for the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, focusing on statues including the Colossus of Rhodes and the Statue of Zeus:

## Colossus of Rhodes

The Colossus of Rhodes was a statue of the Greek sun god Helios, erected in the city of Rhodes by Chares of Lindos in 280 BC, and was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. 

**Height:** According to most contemporary descriptions, the Colossus stood approximately 70 cubits, or 33 metres (108 feet) high—approximately two-thirds of the height of the modern Statue of Liberty from feet to crown—making it the tallest statue in the ancient world.

It collapsed during the earthquake of 226 BC, although parts of it were preserved.

## Statue of Zeus

Chares' teacher, the sculptor Lysippos, had constructed a 22-metre-high (72-foot) bronze statue of Zeus at Tarentum. Another source on the Statue of Zeus at Olympia indicates it stood at an imposing height of 40 feet and was crafted from ivory.

These two statues were among the most impressive sculptures in the ancient world, with the Colossus of Rhodes being significantly taller than the Statue of Zeus.

## Height

The Statue of Zeus at Olympia was a giant seated figure, about 12.4 m (41 ft) tall, made by the Greek sculptor Phidias around 435 BC at the sanctuary of Olympia, Greece. Some sources cite slightly different measurements, ranging from approximately 12 to 13 meters (39-43 feet).

## As an Ancient Wonder

It was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. The statue was a chryselephantine sculpture of ivory plates and gold panels on a wooden framework.

## Key Details

Zeus sat on a painted cedarwood throne ornamented with ebony, ivory, gold, and precious stones. The Greek geographer Strabo wrote that the sculpture was so large that had the god of thunder stood up from his throne, he would 'unroof the temple'.

## Its Fate

The statue was lost and destroyed before the end of the 6th century AD, with conflicting accounts of the date and circumstances. Details of its form are known only from ancient Greek descriptions and representations on coins and art.

## Location and Overview
The Church of Santa María del Azogue is centrally located within the charming town of Betanzos in the A Coruña province of Galicia, Spain. Betanzos, often dubbed the "City of Knights," is a historic gem located in the province of A Coruña, Galicia, Northern Spain.

## Historical Significance
With roots tracing back to pre-Roman times, this town offers a rich mix of history, from its early days as a Roman settlement to its medieval prominence as a key trade center and one of the capitals of the ancient Kingdom of Galicia.

## Catholic Churches and Pilgrimage
Betanzos is home to a total of three monumental Gothic churches that seem a world away from your typical Galician sanctuary. The three main churches are:

1. **Church of Santa María del Azogue** - Built between 14 and 15th Centuries in a Gothic style

2. **Church of San Francisco** - Built in the 14th Century in a Gothic-style, where before there was a monastery. To tour the Church of San Francisco in Betanzos is to walk through a piece of nobility history, as well as to discover one of the greatest collections of medieval funeral sculptures in Spain.

3. **Church of Santiago** - This church is a beautiful example of the transition from the Romanesque to the Gothic style.

Betanzos is worth staying for a few days as you take a break from your Camino Inglés Pilgrimage.

Here's a summary of the search results about Reform Congregation Keneseth Israel in Philadelphia and its rabbinical history:

## Congregation History

Reform Congregation Keneseth Israel (KI) was founded in Philadelphia in 1847 and is recognized as the sixth-oldest Reform congregation in the country. Orthodox in observance at first, KI adopted reform in 1855, and thus became the first progressive congregation in Philadelphia, and only the fifth in the entire country.

## Notable Rabbis

The congregation has been led by eight senior rabbis throughout its history. Key figures include:

- David Einhorn, one of the greatest Jewish intellectuals of his day, a firebrand abolitionist and author of the prayer book which formed the original basis of the Union Prayer Book, was Rabbi from 1861 to 1866.

- He was succeeded by Dr. Samuel Hirsch, the former Chief Rabbi of Luxembourg, who was both a scholar and a pioneer in Jewish social services in Philadelphia.

- Dr. Joseph Krauskopf, a member of the first graduating class of the Hebrew Union College, followed Hirsch. Under Dr. Krauskopf, KI became the largest synagogue in the United States.

- In 1924, Dr. William H. Fineshriber was called to the pulpit of Keneseth Israel. He was the first American-born rabbi to serve the congregation.

- Dr. Fineshriber was succeeded in 1949 by Dr. Bertram W. Korn, who was the first rabbi in American History to have been promoted to "flag" rank as a Rear Admiral in the Navy.

- Rabbi Lance J. Sussman became KI's eighth Senior Rabbi in July, 2001. He earned his Ph.D. in American Jewish History at Hebrew Union College-Jewish Institute of Religion.

results:
Based on the search results, the intertidal zone is broken into three smaller sections called the high intertidal, the mid intertidal, and the low intertidal.

Here's what characterizes each zone:

- **High Intertidal Zone**: Only covered by the highest of the high tides, and spends much of its time as terrestrial habitat. It is inhabited by hardy sea life that can withstand pounding waves, such as barnacles, marine snails, mussels, limpets, shore crabs, and hermit crabs.

- **Mid Intertidal Zone**: Regularly exposed and submerged by average tides. It is inhabited by a greater variety of both plants and animals, including sea stars and anemones.

- **Low Intertidal Zone**: Only exposed to air at the lowest of low tides and is primarily marine in character. Life is more abundant there because of the protection provided by the water.

## Habitat Distribution

Beds of the tropical box mussels are a common feature in the intertidal habitat of North Sulawesi, and box mussel Septifer bilocularis live clustered with very dense aggregations in intertidal reef flat area on the intertidal zone.

## Physical Characteristics

The species is attached to rocks among algae. Additionally, S. bilocularis nestles singly in crevices in coral heads, and mussel beds are found in the centre of the intertidal zone with mangroves between the mussel beds and the mainland.

## Geographic Range

The species is found in tropical Indo-Pacific regions, also in Australia.

## Settlement Behavior

Early settlement occurs when mussels' larvae first settle and attach to coconut, palm, and polypropylene fibres before reattaching to adult shells with byssus threads.

The species is adapted to dynamic intertidal environments where it forms dense clusters among algae and coral structures in wave-exposed areas.

## Adult Tick Seasonal Activity

Adult ticks are most active from March to mid-May and from mid-August to November. In early spring and fall seasons, adults are most active.

## Fall Activity Specifically

Adult ticks take their final blood meal during the fall, with mating typically occurring on a vertebrate host. Additionally, the tick can be active after a hard frost, as daytime temperatures can warm it enough to keep it actively searching for a host.

## Lyme Disease Transmission by Life Stage

While adults are active in the fall, it's important to note that from April through July, nymphs are actively questing for hosts in the environment, and nymphal ticks pose a particularly high risk due to their abundance and small size. Both nymphs and adults can transmit Lyme disease.

The first bank established in the Kingdom of Hawaii was Bishop & Co., founded by Charles Reed Bishop and William A. Aldrich in 1858. First Hawaiian Bank, founded in 1858, is Hawaiʻi's oldest and largest financial institution headquartered in Honolulu.

## Charles Reed Bishop Biography

Charles Reed Bishop (January 25, 1822 – June 7, 1915) was an American businessman, politician, and philanthropist in Hawaii.

### Early Life
Born in Glens Falls, New York, he sailed to Hawaii in 1846 at the age of 24, and made his home there, marrying into the royal family of the kingdom.

Bishop served on the Privy Council for five Hawaiian monarchs from 1859 to 1891, and was Minister of Foreign Affairs from January 10, 1873, to February 17, 1874.

Bishop was one of the first trustees of and major donor to the Kamehameha Schools, founded at his late wife's bequest to provide education to Hawaiian children. He was also a founder of the Bernice Pauahi Bishop Museum, which he named after his late wife.

The average temperature across the Canary Islands archipelago in July 2024 was 23.2°C, which is 0.9°C above the long-term average, making it the tenth warmest July since 1961.

## Key Information About Stephen Etnier

Stephen Morgan Etnier (September 11, 1903 – November 7, 1984) was an American realist painter, and an active painter for six decades.

### Novel Inspiration

Drawing inspiration from The Moon and Sixpence, Somerset Maugham's novel based on the life of the painter Paul Gauguin, Etnier pursued painting, launching his career with a solo exhibition at Dudensing Galleries, New York City in 1931.

### Biography and Autobiography

In his autobiography Overworked Guardian Angel, published posthumously in 2009, the painter Stephen Etnier (1903-1984) paid homage to the stretch of the Maine coast around South Harpswell where he lived and which he haunted for a good part of his life.

### Painting Style and Career

His work is distinguished by a mixture of realism and luminism, favoring industrial and working scenes, but always imbued with atmospheric light. He adopted an artist's discipline of rising early and painting each morning (learned first from Rockwell Kent), seeking to capture the essence of Maine waterfronts and landscapes and the effects of light.

His work appears in the permanent collections of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, Boston Museum of Fine Arts and other museums across the United States.

Based on the search results, the painting stolen from the Louvre on August 21, 1911 was the Mona Lisa, stolen by Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian decorator who had briefly worked at the Louvre as a glazier.

Peruggia entered the Louvre on the morning of August 21, 1911, wearing a white smock like other museum workers, taking advantage of the fact that the museum was closed that day for weekly maintenance during the summer holidays. He lifted the painting off the wall pegs, removed it from its protective case and frame, and hid the discarded elements in a stairwell.

Peruggia claimed he stole the painting for patriotic reasons, believing it had been taken from Italy by Napoleon and wanting to return it to Italy. However, after two years, Peruggia contacted an art dealer in Florence offering to return the painting, was caught, and arrested by police.

The theft had a profound impact: the notoriety from newspaper headlines and the large-scale police investigation helped the Mona Lisa become one of the best known paintings in the world.

Sunday in the Park with George is a 1984 musical with music and lyrics by Stephen Sondheim and book by James Lapine. It was inspired by the French pointillist painter Georges Seurat's painting A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte (painted 1884–1886).

The plot revolves around George, a fictionalized version of Seurat, who immerses himself deeply in painting his masterpiece, and his great-grandson (also named George), a conflicted and cynical contemporary artist.

The musical was highly acclaimed. The musical won the 1985 Pulitzer Prize for Drama, two Tony Awards for design (and a nomination for Best Musical), numerous Drama Desk Awards, the 1991 Olivier Award for Best Musical, and the 2007 Olivier Award for Outstanding Musical Production.

Interestingly, Lapine persuaded [Sondheim] to return to the theatrical world after the two were inspired by A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte, as Sondheim had announced his intention to quit musical theatre after the failure of "Merrily We Roll Along" in 1981.

## Historical Etymology (Old Iranian Origin)

The name Baghlan is possibly derived from the Bactrian term bagolango, meaning "image-temple", which originates from the Old Iranian root baga danaka (Old Persian), referring to a sanctuary or divine shrine, inscribed on the temple of Surkh Kotal during the reign of the Kushan emperor Kanishka in the early 2nd century CE. The name is generally understood to have evolved phonetically into Baghlan.

## Alternative Persian Etymology

A different interpretation suggests the name "Baghlan" is derived from the Persian word "bagh," meaning "garden," and the suffix "-lan," which is a locative suffix. Therefore, Baghlan literally translates to "place of gardens." This name likely reflects the historical agricultural richness and verdant landscapes of the region.

## Historical References

The Chinese Buddhist monk Xuanzang traveled through Baghlan in the mid-7th century CE, and referred to it as the "kingdom of Fo-kia-lang".

The most widely accepted scholarly interpretation traces the name to ancient Old Iranian and Bactrian origins associated with temple sanctuaries, though the Persian meaning relating to gardens also reflects the region's historical agricultural importance.

Based on the search results, here's what we know about the exact date of the Mount Vesuvius eruption in 79 CE:

## The Traditional Date

For more than five centuries, articles about the eruption typically stated that it began on August 24, 79 AD, a date that came from a 1508 printed copy of a letter from Pliny the Younger.

## The Dating Controversy

Manuscript experts believe that the date originally given by Pliny was one of August 24, October 30, November 1, or November 23, with this odd scattered set of dates due to the Romans' convention for describing calendar dates. Over fourteen centuries of manuscript hand-copying up to the 1508 printing of his letters, the date given in Pliny's original letter may have been corrupted.

## Evidence for an October Date

Since at least the late 18th century, some archaeologists have suggested the eruption began in autumn, perhaps in October or November, supported by discoveries of autumnal fruits (such as pomegranates), remains of victims in heavy clothing, and large earthenware storage vessels laden with wine.

In October 2018, Italian archaeologists uncovered a charcoal inscription reading "the 16th day before the calends of November," or October 17, that was probably made just before the eruption of Vesuvius.

A 2007 study of prevailing winds in Campania showed that the southeasterly debris pattern of the first-century eruption is quite consistent with an autumn event and inconsistent with an August date.

The exact date remains debated, with the balance of evidence now pointing to the autumn, perhaps October 24, as the most likely date.

In East Asian Buddhism, Avalokiteśvara is known as 觀音 (an abbreviation for 觀世音), pronounced Gwoon Yaam in Cantonese, Guanyin in Mandarin Chinese, Kannon in Japanese, Gwaneum in Korean, and Quan Âm in Vietnamese.

More specifically:

- **Guanyin** is the Chinese name for the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, meaning "Hearing the Sounds of the World"
- **Kannon** is the Japanese name for Guanyin
- **Avalokiteśvara** is a Bodhisattva associated with Great Compassion (mahākaruṇā)

Among the Chinese, Avalokiteśvara is almost exclusively called Guanshiyin Pusa (觀世音菩薩). The full name Guanshiyin means "Observing the Sounds (or Cries) of the World," with Guanyin being the shortened form commonly used today.

So in summary: Avalokiteśvara is the Sanskrit original name, Guanyin is its Chinese name, and Kannon is its Japanese name—all referring to the same bodhisattva of compassion and mercy.

**Federal Law Violated:** Video Privacy Protection Act (VPPA)

**Ruling Date:** Monday, September 20, 2022

**What Happened:**

Boston Globe Media Partners faced a class action lawsuit filed by subscriber David Ambrose, who alleged the company disclosed his personal information to Facebook without authorization. Based on the search results, here's information about the Ambrose v. Boston Globe Media Partners VPPA case:

## Settlement Details

Boston Globe Media Partners, LLC reached a settlement in the class action lawsuit, Ambrose v. Boston Globe Media Partners, LLC, centered around allegations of the media company violating the Video Privacy Protection Act (VPPA) by disclosing its subscribers' personally identifiable information (PII) to Facebook without consent.

The settlement received final approval on September 8, 2023, with a fund totaling $4,000,000. The settlement includes a $4 million sum to be split among subscribers and an additional $1 million of in-kind payments in the form of one-week extensions to existing subscriptions.

## Case Background

On February 5, 2022, Plaintiff David Ambrose filed a putative class action on behalf of digital subscribers to the Boston Globe who have a Facebook account and viewed videos on Defendant's website pursuant to the Video Privacy Protection Act.

This was the first ever Facebook Tracking Pixel-based VPPA case to be filed across the country, and therefore the case presented novel and complex legal issues.

## Compensation

Class counsel estimates that each claimant will receive between $20 and $40. The fund is designed to compensate those who had a digital subscription to the Boston Globe, a home delivery subscription to the Boston Globe with digital access, or viewed videos on Boston Globe's website from February 5, 2020, to May 25, 2023.

## Settlement Terms

The Boston Globe agreed to stop using Facebook Pixel tracking until they obtain a VPPA-complaint consent disclosure.

Based on the search results, here's what we know about the origins of tennis:

## Early Origins

The game originated in France in the 11th or 12th century and was played by French monks who played handball against the monastery walls or over a rope strung across a courtyard. The game was called 'jeu de paume', meaning 'game of the hand'.

## Modern Lawn Tennis

While tennis has ancient roots in France, the modern form of tennis originated in Birmingham, England, in the late 19th century as lawn tennis. In 1873, Major Walter Clopton Wingfield, an Officer in the British Army was the first to introduce lawn tennis and even created an equipment set that people could buy to play in their gardens.

So to answer your question: **France** is where tennis was first historically played (around the 11th-12th centuries), while **England** is where the modern version we know today originated in the late 19th century.

## Men

The most successful British tennis player of all time was Fred Perry, who is the only Briton to have won all four Grand Slam tournaments. Perry reached 10 Grand Slam finals and won eight between 1933 and 1936, including the last three consecutive Wimbledon titles (1934–1936) and becoming the first British man to complete a career Grand Slam by claiming all four majors.

Andy Murray is the only British player, apart from Fred Perry, to have reached the final of all four Grand Slams. However, it's important to note that Murray has not completed a career Grand Slam—he won the US Open (2012), Wimbledon (2013, 2016), but never won the Australian Open or French Open.

## Women

Angela Mortimer, Ann Haydon-Jones and Virginia Wade each won three of the Grand Slams. While these players won three major titles each, none of them completed a career Grand Slam by winning all four different major tournaments.

In summary, **Fred Perry is the only British player to have won all four Grand Slam singles titles during their career**.

## Architectural Style

The tower was designed by Augustus Pugin and Sir Charles Barry in the Perpendicular Gothic style and was completed in 1859. More specifically, Big Ben was designed in the Gothic Revival style of architecture, which features lancet windows, heavy ornamentation, pinnacles, and the use of natural materials such as stone and iron.

## Key Architectural Features

The design of Big Ben, spearheaded by architect Augustus Pugin, draws on various elements of Gothic architecture, such as pointed arches, spires, and intricate decorative stonework. The tower is richly decorated with carvings, statues, shields, and inscriptions that reflect the history and identity of the United Kingdom.

## Materials and Construction

The bottom 200 feet (61.0 m) of Elizabeth Tower's structure consists of brickwork with sand coloured Anston limestone cladding. The remainder of the tower's height is a framed spire of cast iron.

## Height and Proportions

The tower is designed in Pugin's celebrated Gothic Revival style, and is 315 feet (96.0 m) high (roughly 16 storeys).

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Gothic Revival architecture's first buildings and pioneers in England:

## Early Beginnings

Gothic Revival (also referred to as Victorian Gothic or Neo-Gothic) is an architectural movement that after a gradual build-up beginning in the second half of the 17th century became a widespread movement in the first half of the 19th century, mostly in England.

## Earliest Examples

The earliest documented example of the revived use of Gothic architectural elements is Strawberry Hill, the home of the English writer Horace Walpole. With the rebuilding beginning in 1747 of the country house Strawberry Hill by the English writer Horace Walpole, a new and significant aspect of the revived style was given convincing form.

Another important early example was Fonthill Abbey, designed by James Wyatt, a country house with a tower 270 feet (82 metres) high.

## Pioneering Figures

The most significant pioneer of the Gothic Revival was Augustus Welby Northmore Pugin (1812-1852), the key protagonist for the Gothic Revival by much of Victorian England. After helping his father to survey and record medieval buildings he became convinced that Gothic architecture was not only superior aesthetically, but also morally to Classical architecture. In 1836 he published 'Contrasts', in which he compares different types of contemporary buildings with similar ones from the Middle Ages.

## Major Public Building

The greatest example of authentic Gothic Revival is the Palace of Westminster (The Houses of Parliament). The Palace of Westminster was rebuilt by Sir Charles Barry and A.W. Pugin after a disastrous fire destroyed the old buildings in 1834. While Barry oversaw the construction, much of the design is Pugin's, a design he carried out in exacting Perpendicular Gothic style inside and out.

## Career Overview

Gerald Taggart was born on 18 October 1970 and is a Northern Irish former professional footballer. He played for Barnsley, Bolton Wanderers, Leicester City, Manchester City and Stoke City as well as the Northern Ireland national team.

## Club Career

Taggart began his career as a trainee with Manchester City in 1989 but joined Barnsley in 1990 after being unable to break into the first team at Maine Road. Based on the search results, I found comprehensive information about Coronet Records and the Australian Record Company:

## Coronet Records & Label Design

Coronet was created by ARC as a new imprint for its Columbia products because EMI owned the Columbia trademark in Australia. Coronet quickly became ARC's flagship imprint.

The most distinctive feature of Coronet Records was its label design. It was immediately recognisable by its famous octagonal label, which was apparently the only label of this shape in the history of the industry worldwide.

## Record Series & Releases

There were four series, each indicated by a specific prefix -- Popular (KP and KS), Western (KW) and Children's (KK). The "KP" series (issued on 78rpm) began around the middle of 1956; the "KS" (45rpm) series began some time after, in late 1956 or early 1957.

## Label History

Although the Coronet label carried the CBS logo, and the bulk of Coronet's Popular releases were American recordings sourced from CBS, music historian Hank Facer declares Coronet to be a bona fide indigenous label. ARC also began recording and releasing material by local artists, and according to Hank Facer ARC was second only to Festival in terms of support for local artists in the Fifties.

In 1960 ARC was taken over by CBS Records and the Coronet label was phased out in favour of the new CBS Australia label, which used the CBS/Columbia "walking eye" logo.

## Founding Year and Origins

The Winnipeg Free Press was founded on November 30, 1872, as the Manitoba Free Press by William Fisher Luxton and John A. Kenny. The Free Press was founded in 1872, only two years after Manitoba became part of Canada, in 1870. The newspaper's founding predated Winnipeg's own incorporation, in 1873.

## Historical Significance

The Winnipeg Free Press has since become the oldest newspaper in Western Canada that is still active.

## Name Change

On December 2, 1931, the paper was renamed the Winnipeg Free Press. It had been called the Manitoba Free Press for nearly 60 years prior to this change.

## Key Ownership Changes

About 1892, control of the Free Press passed to Clifford Sifton. From 1901 to 1944, John Wesley Dafoe served as editorial writer, editor-in-chief and president. More recently, in December 2001, the Free Press and its sister paper, Brandon Sun, were bought from Thomson Newspapers by FP Canadian Newspapers Limited Partnership.

## Volcanic Foundation

From mid Eocene (35 Ma) to Oligocene times a submarine volcano built up over a hotspot, and formed a seamount composed of basalt. The seamount rises over 4300 m above the ocean floor.

## Current Geological Status

It's important to note that Nauru does **not** have an active volcano currently. The volcano was eroded to sealevel and a coral atoll grew on top to a thickness of about 500 m. Nauru Island is a raised atoll capping a volcanic seamount rising from an ocean floor depth of 4300 m.

## Island Composition

The original limestone has been dolomitised by magnesium from sea water. The coral was raised above sea level about 30 m, and is now a dolomite limestone outcrop which was eroded in classic karst style into pinnacles up to 20 m high.

## Geological Features

Anibare Bay was formed by the underwater collapse of the east side of the volcano. The collapse formed an amphitheatre shape with the arc shaped block rotating outwards at its base from about 900 to 1100 m below sea level.

So while Nauru has a volcanic origin, it is now an ancient, extinct volcano that has been heavily modified by coral growth, erosion, and karst dissolution processes.

Based on the search results, here's what we know about when calculus was invented:

## Development Timeline

Infinitesimal calculus was developed in the late 17th century by Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz independently of each other.

**Newton's Work:**
Newton began working on a form of calculus (which he called "The Method of Fluxions and Infinite Series") in 1666, at the age of 23. While Newton began development of his fluxional calculus in 1665–1666 his findings did not become widely circulated until later.

**Leibniz's Work:**
Gottfried Leibniz began working on his variant of calculus in 1674, and in 1684 published his first paper employing it, "Nova Methodus pro Maximis et Minimis".

## Publication History

Leibniz was the first to publish his investigations; however, it is well established that Newton had started his work several years prior to Leibniz and had already developed a theory of tangents by the time Leibniz became interested in the question.

## The Controversy

Historically, there was much debate over whether it was Newton or Leibniz who first "invented" calculus. This argument, the Leibniz and Newton calculus controversy, involving Leibniz, who was German, and the Englishman Newton, led to a rift in the European mathematical community lasting over a century.

The death toll from the Bath School disaster on May 18, 1927, is reported differently depending on the source and timing:

## Length and Circuit Distance

The York Medieval Walls are approximately 2 miles (3.4 kilometres) long, making them the longest town walls in England. The full circuit of the York City Walls takes approximately 2 hours to complete.

## Key Features

There are five main "bars" (big gateways), one postern (a small gateway), and 45 towers along the walls. The walls are generally 13 feet (4 m) high and 6 feet (1.8 m) wide.

## Historical Significance

Construction of the walls began in Roman times around the 3rd century AD, and in the 12th century, the walls were rebuilt using stone by the Normans. During the medieval period, the walls were strengthened with additional towers and gates, including the famous Micklegate Bar and Monk Bar.

## Early Brand Launches

In 1954 the company branched out from denim to the sportswear business, launching Lighter Blues, a line of casual slacks for men.

However, the most significant early brand extension was Dockers, introduced in the United States in 1986; the brand was released in Europe in 1994. Dockers was one of the most successful brand launches in the history of the American apparel industry.

## Later Brand Launches

Following Dockers, the company expanded its brand portfolio with:

- In 1996 Levi's Vintage Clothing (LVC)—a line of reproductions of clothing items from the Levi Strauss Archives—was introduced worldwide.

- The company later launched (2003) the Signature by Levi Strauss & Co. brand, a more affordable line of jeans and casual wear.

- On August 5, 2021, Levi Strauss & Co. announced the acquisition of Beyond Yoga, entering the activewear market.

So while Lighter Blues in 1954 was technically their first new brand, Dockers in 1986 became their most successful brand extension beyond their core denim business.

## Tournament History

The Phoenix Open dates back to 1932 and 1933, when it was known as the Arizona Open. The inaugural Arizona Open / Phoenix Open Winner was Ralph Guldahl. The event rose from the ashes in 1939 when Bob Goldwater Sr. convinced his civic group, The Thunderbirds, to sponsor a golf event.

The tournament has been held at multiple venues over the years. Finally, in 1987, it moved to the now famous TPC Scottsdale, with its circus par three 16th.

## Multiple Winners

Four players have won this event on three different occasions, Gene Littler (1955,1959,1969), Arnold Palmer (1961,1962,1963), Mark Calcavecchia (1989,1992,2001), and Phil Mickelson (1996,2005, 2013).

## Recent Winners

In the 2025 WM Phoenix Open, Thomas Detry defeated Michael Kim and Daniel Berger by a margin of seven strokes.

The tournament is known as "The Greatest Show on Grass" and made it one of the most popular events on the PGA Tour calendar due to its relaxed and festive atmosphere.

## First Race Year and Early History

Benetton Formula Limited was a Formula One constructor that participated from 1986 to 2001. In 1985, the Benetton family acquired the Toleman team, which had been operating in Formula One since 1981, and following the acquisition, the team was rebranded as Benetton Formula Ltd in early 1986.

## Background and Development

The Benetton Group entered Formula One as a sponsor company for constructor Tyrrell in 1983, then Alfa Romeo in 1984 and 1985 and finally Toleman in 1985. The team retained many of Toleman's key personnel, including designer Rory Byrne and technical director Pat Symonds, who would play pivotal roles in the team's future successes.

## Success and Championships

The Benetton team is today best known for its success with Michael Schumacher, who accounts for 19 of the team's 27 race victories and their two World Drivers' Championships. Michael Schumacher won his first Drivers' Championships with the team in 1994 and 1995, and the team won their only Constructors' title in 1995.

## End of the Benetton Era

In 2000, the team was purchased by Renault, but competed as Benetton for the 2000 and 2001 seasons. In 2002, the team became Renault.

Here's what I found about the 1996 Formula One World Championship and Damon Hill's first title with Williams:

## Damon Hill's Historic Championship

Damon Hill won the Formula One World Drivers' Championship in 1996 with Williams, achieving a historic milestone. Damon Hill won the Drivers' Championship two years after being beaten by a point by Michael Schumacher, making him the first son of a World Champion (his father Graham having won the title in 1962 and 1968) to have won the title himself.

## The Championship Campaign

The Williams car was clearly the quickest in Formula One and Hill went on to win the title ahead of his teammate, reigning Indycar champion Jacques Villeneuve. Hill, who had finished runner-up for the past two seasons, was seriously threatened only by his teammate, newcomer Jacques Villeneuve, the 1995 IndyCar and Indianapolis 500 champion.

## The Decisive Race

Damon Hill made Formula 1 history on this day 28 years ago underneath a sunny sky in Suzuka for the 1996 Japanese Grand Prix. Driving his FW18 in the lead of all 52 laps, the British racer became the first driver in F1 history to follow in their parent's footsteps and become a champion child of another title-winning driver. Hill took the lead at the start and won both the race and the championship while the Canadian retired.

## Team and Legacy

Williams-Renault easily won the Constructors' title, as there was no other competitor strong enough to post a consistent challenge throughout the championship. Despite his success, Hill and designer Adrian Newey would depart at the conclusion of the season, with engine manufacturer Renault also leaving after 1997.

## Species Information

The brown rhinoceros beetle (*Xylotrupes gideon*) is a species of large scarab beetle belonging to the subfamily Dynastinae.

## Size and Length

*Xylotrupes gideon* can reach a length of 3.5–7 centimetres (1.4–2.8 in). As usual with rhinoceros beetles there is a great difference between the genders, with males being larger than females.

## Physical Characteristics

These beetles are shiny dark red, dark brown, or black in coloration. They have two chitinous bifurcated horns, a thick thoracic horn and a smaller cephalic horn, which they use to eliminate their rivals during the mating period.

## Geographic Distribution

This species is widespread in India, Sri Lanka, Thailand, Indonesia: Java (nominotypical form), Borneo (borneensis), Sunda Islands and Moluccas.

## Sikh Empire Capital

Lahore was the Sikh empire's capital. Following the Battle of Sobraon, Lahore fell under British control on February 20, 1846.

## Battle of Sobraon (1846)

The Battle of Sobraon was fought on 10 February 1846, between the forces of the East India Company and the Sikh Khalsa Army, the army of the declining Sikh Empire of the Punjab. The Sikhs were completely defeated, making this the decisive battle of the First Anglo-Sikh War.

The battle had significant consequences for the Sikh Empire. On 13 February, Gough's army was only 30 miles from Lahore, the Sikh empire's capital, and although detachments of the Khalsa remained intact in outlying frontier districts of the Punjab, they could not be concentrated quickly enough to defend Lahore. 

By the Treaty of Lahore, the Sikhs ceded the valuable agricultural lands of the Bist Doab (Jullundur Doab) (between the Beas and Sutlej Rivers) to the East India Company, and allowed a British Resident at Lahore with subordinates in other principal cities.

## Punjab Annexation and British Crown Rule

Most of the Punjab region was annexed by the British East India Company on 29 March 1849, making it one of the last areas of the Indian subcontinent to fall under British control.

In 1858, the Punjab, along with the rest of British India, came under the rule of the British Crown. This marked a significant transition from Company rule to direct Crown rule.

## Lahore Specifically

Lahore served as an important administrative and commercial center under the Mughal Empire (1526–1799), the Sikh Empire (1799–1849), the British East India Company (1849–1858), and the British government (1858–1947) when it took direct control of India.

Under the terms of the Queen's Proclamation issued by Queen Victoria, the Punjab, along with the rest of British India, came under the direct rule of the British Crown. The East India Company was abolished, along with its court of directors, replacing that administrative set-up with the council of India.

## Overall Head-to-Head Record

Venus and Serena met 31 times in professional tournaments between 1998 and 2020, with Serena leading their overall head-to-head 19–12.

## First Matches

Serena and Venus Williams played their first professional match against each other in the second round of the 1998 Australian Open, with Venus winning 7–6(4), 6–1. 

They played again in the quarterfinals of the Italian Open, the first clay court tournament of Serena's career, which Venus won 6–4, 6–2.

Venus ultimately won that match and would capture five of the first six head-to-head meetings (not counting Serena's infamous walkover win at the 2001 Indian Wells).

Serena's best winning streak in the H2H was six across 2002 and 2003, while Venus never bettered her 3-0 start to the rivalry.

The most recent encounter between them was on 13-08-2020 in the Second Round at the The Top Seed Open - Lexington, where Serena won 3-6 6-3 6-4.

Based on the search results, here's information about the Crab Nebula supernova remnant:

## Overview

The Crab Nebula is the shattered remnant of a massive star that ended its life in a massive supernova explosion. Nearly a thousand years old, the supernova was noted in the constellation of Taurus by Chinese astronomers in the year 1054 AD.

## Physical Characteristics

The nebula is about 6,500 light-years away from the Earth, and is 5 light-years across. The nebula, 6,500 light-years away, is expanding at 1,100 km (700 miles) per second.

## Structure and Composition

The much fainter remnant observed today is an expanding shell of gas and dust, and outflowing wind powered by a pulsar, a rapidly spinning and highly magnetized neutron star. The blue region traces the cloud of energetic electrons trapped within the star's magnetic field, emitting so-called "synchrotron" radiation.

## Scientific Significance

The Crab Nebula was the first astronomical object recognized as being connected to a supernova explosion. The Crab is one of the few astronomical objects from which radiation has been detected over the entire measurable spectrum, from radio waves through infrared and visible wavelengths to ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays.

## Recent Discoveries

In June 2021, scientists announced they'd finally found evidence for a new type of supernova, an electron-capture supernova. Consequently, they now believe the Crab nebula may be this type of supernova.

## Main Successor Institution

Prince of Wales College merged with St. Dunstan's University in 1969 to form the University of Prince Edward Island (UPEI). In May 1969 the last classes graduated from PWC and SDU and the institutions were merged into the University of Prince Edward Island which opened for the first time in September 1969 on the now-former SDU campus.

## Secondary Use of PWC Campus

The PWC campus on Grafton Street was taken over by the provincial government and became the Charlottetown campus of a new provincial community college named Holland College. Holland College was formed by the Government of Prince Edward Island in 1969 as a result of an education reform policy which saw the closure of the province's two post-secondary institutions structured on religious lines, St. Dunstan's University and Prince of Wales College, and the creation of the non-denominational University of Prince Edward Island (UPEI) and Holland College.

So while the primary successor was UPEI (a university), Holland College (a community college) was created to serve different educational needs and eventually occupied the former PWC campus.

## Founder of Bilbao

Bilbao was founded in 1300 by Diego López V de Haro, who was lord of Biscay and gave the settlement the charter and privilege of self-government in an independent municipality. The wolves on the city's coat of arms represent the founder, as "Lope" comes from the Latin lupus meaning 'wolf'.

## Early History

Bilbao originated as a settlement of seafaring people on the banks of the Nervión's estuary, and the inhabitants began to export both the iron ore found in large quantities along the river's eastern bank and the products of their ironworks.

## Development Through the Centuries

In 1602, Bilbao was made the capital of Biscay, a title previously held by Bermeo. In the 18th century, Bilbao derived great prosperity from intensive trade with the American colonies of Spain.

The city experienced significant transformation in the 19th and 20th centuries. Throughout the nineteenth century and the beginning of the twentieth, Bilbao experienced heavy industrialisation, making it the centre of the second-most industrialised region of Spain, behind Barcelona. In more recent times, Bilbao is a vigorous service city that is experiencing an ongoing social, economic, and aesthetic revitalisation process, started by the iconic Bilbao Guggenheim Museum.

Robert Emory Pattison was an American attorney and politician who served as the 19th governor of Pennsylvania from 1883 to 1887 and 1891 to 1895. He was the Democratic candidate for governor at the young age of 32, and, with little experience in public office, took the governor's office back from a succession of Republican administrations.

Pattison was the only Democratic Governor of Pennsylvania between the start of the American Civil War and the Great Depression era. Under the constitution of 1874, Pennsylvania governors, now serving a 4-year term, were prevented from seeking two consecutive terms. Pattison's opponent in the 1882 election, James Addams Beaver, held the post for a term before Pattison sought the office once again in 1890.

During his time as governor, Pattison focused on fiscal responsibility, advocating an end to patronage, graft, and corruption. He also sought to curtail corporate power, the divisions between labor and capital, and the railroads' monopolistic controls.

The dam was constructed between 1931 and 1936, during the Great Depression, with work beginning in 1931, not 1936. However, regarding the two names: Bills passed by Congress during its construction referred to it as Hoover Dam (after President Herbert Hoover), but the Roosevelt administration named it Boulder Dam.

The naming history is interesting: When construction of the dam was initiated on September 30, 1930, Secretary of the Interior Ray Lyman Wilbur ordered that the dam be called Hoover Dam, and by a Congressional Act of February 14, 1931, this name was made official. However, following Hoover's defeat by Franklin D. Roosevelt in the 1932 presidential election, the Roosevelt Administration began calling the structure Boulder Dam. 

In 1947, Congress restored the name Hoover Dam.

# Who Created the Typhoid Vaccine?

Based on the article, **Sir Almroth Wright** is primarily credited with creating the first effective typhoid vaccine. The text states that "Wright was responsible for designing the actual vaccine."

Wright, a British pathologist and professor at the Army Medical School in Netley, developed the vaccination around 1896. The article emphasizes that "his persistence in the face of numerous obstacles resulted in the first wide-scale vaccination campaign against typhoid fever in the British and Indian armies."

While **Richard Pfeiffer**, a German bacteriologist, contributed foundational immunology research that made the vaccine possible, Wright receives primary credit for designing and implementing the actual vaccine.

## Hun Invasions of the Gupta Empire

In the late 490's the Alchon Huns under Toramana and Mihirakula broke through the Gupta defences in the northwest, and much of the empire in the northwest was overrun by the Huns by 500.

The Hun invasions occurred in waves. The Hephthalites broke through the Gupta military defenses in the northwest in the 480s, during the reign of Budhagupta, and by 500 CE much of the empire in northwest was overrun by the Huna.

## Consequences of the Invasion

The empire thereafter disintegrated into numerous regional kingdoms, ruled by chieftains. After 515, they absorbed the Kashmir, and they advanced into the Ganges Valley, the heart of India, "raping, burning, massacring, blotting out entire cities and reducing fine buildings to rubble" according to Indian historians.

Eventually, the Huns were defeated and driven out of India in 528 by King Yashodharman from Malwa, and possibly Gupta emperor Narasimhagupta. However, the Gupta Empire ended in 550 CE, when it disintegrated into regional kingdoms after a series of weak rulers and invasions from the east, west, and north.

## Closest Living Relatives to Sirenians

The order Sirenia's closest living relatives are elephants of the order Proboscidea. Sirenians are classified in the clade Paenungulata, alongside the elephants and the hyraxes, and evolved in the Eocene 50 million years ago.

Within the order Sirenia itself, dugongs and manatees are both part of the order Sirenia, which includes one dugong species and three species of manatees. Here's what I found regarding the discovery history of these three antileprosy drugs:

## Clofazimine

Clofazimine, initially known as B663, was first synthesized in 1954 by a team of scientists at Trinity College, Dublin, led by Vincent Barry. Clofazimine was originally intended as an anti-tuberculosis drug but proved ineffective. In 1959, a researcher named Y. T. Chang identified its effectiveness against leprosy.

## Dapsone

The first antibiotic to be widely used for leprosy treatment was dapsone in the 1950s, which had to be taken over several years and was associated with increasing bacterial resistance.

## Rifampicin

In the early 1960s, rifampicin and clofazimine were discovered and subsequently added to the treatment regimen, which was later labelled as multidrug therapy (MDT). In 1981, WHO recommended that all registered patients with leprosy should receive combination therapy with three antibiotics: rifampicin, clofazimine, and dapsone.

**Discovery of Rifamycin (Precursor):**
In 1957, a research group led by Piero Sensi discovered a new antibiotic which they named rifamycin, isolated from cultures of Amycolatopsis rifamycinica. A soil sample from a pine forest on the French Riviera was brought for analysis to the Lepetit Pharmaceuticals research lab in Milan, Italy, where a research group headed by Piero Sensi and Maria Teresa Timbal discovered a new bacterium, Nocardia mediterranei.

**Synthesis of Rifampicin/Rifampin:**
The antibiotic rifampicin was synthesized in 1965 by researchers at Lepetit Pharmaceuticals in Milan, evolving from earlier rifamycin compounds. Rifampin was first synthesized in 1965 and was found to be chemically stable, less toxic to humans, and exhibit activity against a broad spectrum of bacteria.

**Clinical Introduction:**
Rifampicin was first sold in Italy in 1968 and was approved by the FDA in 1971.

**Etymology Note:**
The name rifampin is used in the United States, while the drug is called rifampicin in Europe and Australia.

Based on the search results, here's the history of the City of London Police founding:

## City of London Police Founding History

The City of London Police was formed during 1839, ten years after the Metropolitan Police, with the first Commissioner, Daniel Whittle-Harvey, being responsible for around 500 officers.

However, the origins trace back slightly earlier: The London City Police was officially formed in 1832, before becoming the City of London Police with the passing of the City of London Police Act 1839.

### Background Context

The establishment of the City of London Police was prompted by the success of the Metropolitan Police. When Sir Robert Peel established the Metropolitan Police in 1829, the City of London resisted his attempts to consolidate the policing of the City and greater London with one force. The Mayor and Corporation of the City of London refused to be part of a London-wide force because the City of London had certain liberties dating back to Magna Carta.

This led to the creation of an independent police force for the Square Mile of the City of London, which remains separate from the Metropolitan Police to this day.

Based on the search results, the design of the Eiffel Tower is attributed to Maurice Koechlin and Émile Nouguier, two senior engineers working for the Compagnie des Établissements Eiffel. 

More specifically, in May 1884, working at home, Koechlin made a sketch of their idea, described by him as "a great pylon, consisting of four lattice girders standing apart at the base and coming together at the top, joined together by metal trusses at regular intervals".

Eiffel initially showed little enthusiasm, but he did approve further study, and the two engineers then asked Stephen Sauvestre, the head of the company's architectural department, to contribute to the design. Sauvestre added decorative arches to the base of the tower, a glass pavilion to the first level, and other embellishments.

I found search results about the Legion of Honour medal. Here are the key findings:

## Medal Badge Shape
The badge of the Légion is shaped as a five-armed "Maltese Asterisk", using five distinctive "arrowhead" shaped arms inspired by the Maltese Cross.

## Medal Grades
The original grades were Collar, Grand Eagle (1805), Commandant, Officer, and Legion.

## Models and Variations
During the First Empire (1804-1813), several models are known: the "Large Head" model features a large facing-right portrait of Napoleon on the obverse with a facing-left eagle on the reverse; the "Small Head" model features a small facing-right portrait of Napoleon on the obverse with a facing-left eagle on the reverse; the second "Small Head" model features a medium facing-right portrait of Napoleon on the obverse with a large facing-right eagle on the reverse; and the "Biennais" model features a large facing-right portrait of Napoleon with enameled laurel crown on the obverse with a facing-left eagle on the reverse.

## Hanging Device and Crown
The 'bélière' (the boss linking the medal to the ribbon which appeared on later models, sometimes in the form of a crown) and the centre of the star were modified according to the different political regimes in France. Different eras featured different hanging devices: an imperial crown in the Late Empire, a royal crown in the Louis XVIII era, and a crown of laurels in the Fifth Republic.

## May 12, 1916 Executions

On May 12, 1916, Seán Mac Diarmada and James Connolly were executed by firing squad at Kilmainham Gaol.

### Notable Details

James Connolly was grievously ill and unable to stand in front of the firing squad. More specifically, Connolly was brought to Kilmainham jail in an ambulance, carried to the execution yard on a stretcher, and shot by firing squad while tied to a chair. During the Easter Rising, James Connolly served as Vice-President of the Irish Republic and Commandant-General of the Dublin Division of the Army of the Irish Republic.

### Context

14 men total were executed in Kilmainham Gaol for their involvement in the recent Dublin rebellion, with executions carried out by firing squad at dawn. The executions began on May 3 with Patrick Pearse, Thomas Clarke and Thomas MacDonagh; followed by Joseph Plunkett, Edward Daly, Michael O'Hanrahan and Willie Pearse on May 4; John MacBride on May 5; Éamonn Ceannt, Michael Mallin, Seán Heuston and Con Colbert on May 8; and finally Seán Mac Diarmada and James Connolly on May 12.

The genus Morus comprises about 10 species of small to medium-sized trees, though the exact number is debated. ## Order Composition

Rosales comprise nine families: Barbeyaceae, Cannabaceae, Dirachmaceae, Elaeagnaceae, Moraceae, Rhamnaceae, Rosaceae, Ulmaceae, and Urticaceae.

## Phylogenetic Structure

Within Rosales, all family relationships are well-supported with Rosaceae sister to all other members of the order. Remaining Rosales can be divided into two subclades: 1) Ulmaceae are sister to Cannabaceae plus (Urticaceae + Moraceae); 2) Rhamnaceae are sister to Elaeagnaceae plus (Barbeyaceae + Dirachmaceae).

## The Urticalean Rosids Clade

Four families of the Rosales — Cannabaceae, Moraceae, Ulmaceae, and Urticaceae — comprise a monophyletic group, sometimes referred to as the Urticalean Rosids. Notably, this group is characterized by small, unisexual, wind-pollinated flowers.

## Molecular Basis

Two nuclear and 10 plastid loci were used to infer phylogenetic relationships among all nine families of Rosales, providing the well-supported phylogenetic framework described above.

## Wimbledon's Beginning

The first Wimbledon Tennis Championship took place on July 9, 1877, in Wimbledon, a district now part of Greater London, England. This inaugural event was organized shortly after Major Walter Clopton Wingfield formalized the rules of lawn tennis in 1873.

## Tournament Details

The championship featured a mere 22 male contestants, and the final match saw W. Spencer Gore defeat William Marshall in front of a crowd of about 200 spectators. In a final that lasted only 48 minutes, the 27-year-old Gore dominated with his strong volleying game, crushing Marshall, 6-1, 6-2, 6-4.

## Notable Facts

Women were not permitted to compete in the tournament until seven years later. The club decided to host an annual tennis Championship for gentlemen with the aim of raising funds for its broken pony-drawn roller used to maintain the croquet lawns.

Semifinals were held on July 12, but then the tournament was suspended to leave the London sporting scene free for the Eton vs. Harrow cricket match played on Friday and Saturday. The final was scheduled for Monday, July 16, but, in what would become a common occurrence in future Wimbledon tournaments, the match was rained out.

## Overview

The Dominican Sisters of Hawthorne were founded on December 8, 1900, by Rose Hawthorne Lathrop, a daughter of the famed novelist Nathaniel Hawthorne. They specialize in caring for those suffering from terminal cancer and have no financial resources.

## Rose Hawthorne Lathrop's Background

Rose Hawthorne Lathrop, OP, also known as Mother Mary Alphonsa (May 20, 1851 – July 9, 1926), was an American Dominican religious sister, writer, social worker, and foundress of the Dominican Sisters of Hawthorne. She learned of the plight of the poor who were diagnosed with incurable cancer. At the time, this disease was believed by many to be highly contagious, so there was a deep fear of contact with those suffering from this affliction.

## Her Nursing Work

In the fall of 1896, after having taken a three-month nursing course at New York's Cancer Hospital, Lathrop moved into a three-room cold-water flat on New York City's impoverished Lower East Side and began to nurse the poor with incurable cancer.

## Mission Today

The congregation's apostolate is to provide nursing care to those afflicted with incurable cancer, who are unable to afford nursing care elsewhere. Their homes are free of charge and the sisters provide direct patient care.

## Match Overview

In late 1858, Anderssen was beaten 8–3 by the American champion Paul Morphy in a famous match held in Paris, France (two wins, two draws, seven losses). The match between Morphy and Anderssen took place between December 20, 1858, and December 28, 1858, when Morphy was still only 21 years of age.

## Remarkable Circumstances

Despite the decisive outcome, the match took place under unusual circumstances. In Paris, Morphy suffered from a bout of gastroenteritis. In accordance with the medical wisdom of the time, he was treated with leeches, resulting in his losing a significant amount of blood. Although too weak to stand up unaided, Morphy insisted on going ahead with a match against the visiting German master Adolf Anderssen, considered by many to be Europe's leading player.

## Impact on Chess History

Anderssen is generally regarded as having been the world's leading chess player from 1851 to 1858, but this match marked a turning point. When asked about his defeat, Anderssen claimed to be out of practice, but also admitted that Morphy was in any event the stronger player and that he was fairly beaten. Anderssen also attested that in his opinion, Morphy was the strongest player ever to play the game, even stronger than the famous French champion La Bourdonnais.

The flag of Lesotho, adopted on the 40th anniversary of Lesotho's independence on 4 October 2006, features a horizontal blue, white, and green tricolour with a black mokorotlo (a Basotho hat) in the center. ## Color Meanings

Each color carries symbolic significance:

- The blue color at the top of Lesotho's flag symbolizes the sky and rain.
- The white color in the middle represents peace and people's aspirations for unity.
- The green color signifies the prosperity and richness of the land.

In the middle of the flag, there is a black emblem that features a black Basotho hat at its center, or a "Mokorotlo." The black color was chosen to represent Lesotho as a black nation. ## 2008-09 Playoff Results

The Trail Blazers returned to the postseason for three consecutive years beginning in 2008–09, marking their first playoff appearance after a five-year absence. They were surprised and bullied by the more experienced Houston Rockets, enduring a six-game series loss.

## 2010-11 Playoff Results

The Blazers won 48 games, securing another playoff berth but were eliminated in the first round by the eventual champion Dallas Mavericks in six games.

## 2013-14 Playoff Results

Aldridge's tenure with the Blazers peaked in the spring of 2014, when Portland defeated the Houston Rockets 4-2 in the first round of the 2014 NBA Playoffs. On April 20, 2014, Aldridge recorded a new career high and franchise playoff high of 46 points along with 18 rebounds in Game 1, and on April 23, 2014, he tallied 43 points and eight rebounds in Game 2 of the Blazers' series against the Houston Rockets. The Blazers would lose to the San Antonio Spurs in the second round that year.

President Donald Trump signed the act into law on February 22, 2018, officially renaming the site Gateway Arch National Park. This made it the 60th national park in the United States.

It's worth noting that this was a redesignation rather than a completely new establishment. In its initial form as a national memorial, it was established in 1935 to commemorate the Louisiana Purchase and subsequent westward movement of American explorers and pioneers. The area surrounding the arch was redesignated as the Gateway Arch National Park in 2018.

Michael John Keane is a Canadian former professional ice hockey winger born May 29, 1967. He was born in Winnipeg, Canada.

Undrafted, Keane played over 1,100 games in the National Hockey League from 1988 until 2004. He is a three-time Stanley Cup champion, having won with the Montreal Canadiens in 1993, Colorado Avalanche in 1996, and the Dallas Stars in 1999.

Chairing the Member is an 1828 oil painting by the British artist Benjamin Robert Haydon. Combining elements of genre painting and history painting, it was inspired by an event he has witnessed while imprisoned in the King's Bench Prison for debt. Based on the search results, here is a list of people who have won two Nobel Prizes:

## Nobel Prize Two-Time Winners

Two laureates have been awarded twice but not in the same field: Marie Curie (Physics and Chemistry) and Linus Pauling (Chemistry and Peace). Additionally, the Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to John Bardeen twice, as was the Nobel Prize in Chemistry to Frederick Sanger and Karl Barry Sharpless.

Here's a detailed breakdown:

1. **Marie Curie** - She won her first prize for her work on radioactivity (physics), and then her second a mere eight years later for discovering the elements radium and polonium (chemistry). Among laureates she is the first woman, first double winner, and the first (and only) in two different scientific fields.

2. **Linus Pauling** - The US chemist is the only person to have been awarded two unshared Nobel Prizes—the 1954 Nobel Prize in Chemistry and the 1962 Nobel Peace Prize.

3. **John Bardeen** - He was the first to receive two prizes in the same field (Physics in 1956 and 1972).

4. **Frederick Sanger** - Won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in both 1958 and 1980.

He defeated 18 men during The Streak, which included three bouts with Triple H and two each opposite Kane and Shawn Michaels as well as a handicap match against A-Train and Big Show at WrestleMania XIX.

Here are the key details about Galileo's middle finger and its exhibition history:

## How the Finger Was Obtained

In 1737, 95 years after Galileo died, his remains were transferred to a mausoleum at the Basilica di Santa Croce in Florence. Antiquarian Anton Francesco Gori, anatomist Antonio Cocchi, and Italian marquis Vincenzio Capponi removed the finger of Galileo's right hand as well as one of his vertebrae, an index finger, a thumb, and a tooth.

## Exhibition History

The middle finger was later acquired by Angelo Maria Bandini of the Laurentian Library, where it was exhibited. In 1841, the finger was moved to the Tribune of Galileo at the Museum of Physics and Nature (now La Specola) along with Galileo's Medici-Lorraine instruments. It was then transferred to the Institute and Museum of the History of Science in 1927. In 2010, following a renovation, the palazzo formerly known as the Istituto e Museo di Storia della Scienze reopened as the Museo Galileo.

## Display and Significance

The finger is encased in an egg-shaped glass display above a cylindrical marble base. The base includes a commemorative inscription by astronomer Tommaso Perelli. According to the museum, Galileo's middle finger "exemplifies the celebration of Galileo as a hero and martyr of science".

The Laurentian Library was commissioned in 1523 and construction began in 1525. Built in a cloister of the Medicean Basilica di San Lorenzo di Firenze under the patronage of the Medici pope Clement VII, the library was built to emphasize that the Medici were no longer just merchants but members of intelligent and ecclesiastical society.

When Michelangelo left Florence in 1534, only the walls of the reading room were complete. It was then continued by Tribolo, Vasari, and Ammannati based on plans and verbal instructions from Michelangelo.

The library opened by 1571. The Laurentian Library (Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana or BML) is a historic library in Florence, Italy, containing more than 11,000 manuscripts and 4,500 early printed books. It contains the manuscripts and books belonging to the private library of the Medici family.

## Overview

Alien 3 is a 1992 American science fiction horror film directed by David Fincher and written by David Giler, Walter Hill, and Larry Ferguson, from a story by Vincent Ward. Fincher, in his feature directorial debut, was eventually brought in to direct after a proposed version with Ward as director was canceled during pre-production.

## Release and Reception

Alien 3 was released on May 22, 1992. While it underperformed at the American box office, it earned over $100 million outside North America. The film received mixed reviews and was regarded as inferior to previous installments. Fincher has since disowned the film, deeming it unfaithful to his original vision due to studio interference.

## Production Challenges

Alien3 had a notoriously difficult production. Multiple screenwriters and directors were involved in the film's development, while shooting eventually started at Pinewood Studios without a finished script. Studio interference was extreme — the director's ideas for the production were routinely vetoed by executives who merely wanted to turn out a film on time and under budget.

## Legacy

In 2003, an Assembly Cut without Fincher's involvement was released, featuring alternate scenes and an extended runtime.

## The Sinking of Hiyō

Hiyō was sunk by a gasoline-vapour explosion caused by an American torpedo hit during the Battle of the Philippine Sea on 20 June 1944 with the loss of 247 officers and ratings, about a fifth of her complement.

More specifically, the carrier Hiyō was attacked and hit by bombs and aerial torpedoes from four Grumman TBF Avengers from Belleau Wood, and was set afire after a tremendous blast from leaking aviation fuel. Dead in the water, she sank stern first, with the loss of 250 officers and men, while the rest of her crew, about one thousand, were rescued by Japanese destroyers.

## Carrier Division Assignment

The 652nd Naval Air Group was assigned to the Second Carrier Division with Hiyō, Jun'yō and Ryūhō. This was part of a broader Japanese Navy restructuring where one air group was assigned to one carrier division.

## Battle Context

The Battle of the Philippine Sea was a major naval battle of World War II on 19–20 June 1944 that eliminated the Imperial Japanese Navy's ability to conduct large-scale carrier actions, taking place during the United States' amphibious reconquest of the Mariana Islands during the Pacific War.

results:
Based on the search results, here's what I found about Hoxie Arkansas school integration and desegregation history in the 1950s:

## Overview

The Hoxie story is one of the earliest, most important, and least remembered school integration battles in the South. The first battle to implement the Brown vs Board of Education school desegregation decision was fought in the small, rural town of Hoxie, Arkansas.

## The Desegregation Decision

In the summer of 1955, the school board of a small, rural Arkansas town in Lawrence County voluntarily desegregated its schools, and they were the first to be challenged. Superintendent Vance gave three reasons for integration – he believed it was "right in the sight of God;" he believed it met and complied with the Supreme Court decision in Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka, Kansas; and it saved the school district money.

## Initial Integration

On the morning of July 11, 1955, the black children came to the white Hoxie schools. No incidents occurred on the first day of integration. July 11th was the first day, when 25 African-American students entered the doors of the new school of 1,000 white students in a peaceful and orderly way. Only 21 had attended for one year or more, thus they became known as the Hoxie 21.

## Segregationist Opposition

On Monday, July 25, 1955, however, the situation changed as the latest issue of Life magazine appeared on newsstands across America. The intent of Life's pictorial essay was to recognize a small Southern community's efforts toward compliance with the law. The effect, however, was a spotlight on Hoxie, which attracted the vocal ire of segregationists in the community, and soon in the state and region.

On August 3, 1955, approximately 350 segregationists from the local area gathered in Hoxie City Hall to protest the desegregation of Hoxie schools.

## Legal Outcome

In November 1955, U.S. District Judge Thomas C. Trimble issued a temporary restraining order against the segregationists, stating that the group "planned and conspired" to prevent integration in Hoxie. In December, the court made the temporary order permanent. The office of Attorney General Herbert Brownell, through the U.S. Department of Justice, entered the case on the side of the Hoxie School District. It was a historic move … the first instance of an attorney general siding with a school attempting to comply with Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka, Kansas. Sixteen months later, on Oct. 25, 1956, the court ruled in favor of the Hoxie School.

## Historical Significance

The segregationists' setback at Hoxie was a turning point in their efforts to prevent integration in Arkansas. Because efforts to pressure the school board had failed, the strategy of segregationists changed. No longer would school boards be the primary target, but rather Arkansas politicians.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about the Skyhook extraction scene in The Dark Knight:

## The Scene

In The Dark Knight, Batman infiltrates a secure building and captures a criminal who had fled the United States, then makes his escape by deploying a balloon tethered to him that is snatched out mid-air by a passing aircraft. The scene involves Batman using the skyhook system to extract Lau from Hong Kong.

## The Real Technology

What's remarkable is that this isn't pure fiction. The scene was actually based directly on a very real CIA program called Skyhook (also known as the Fulton surface-to-air recovery system).

The Fulton Skyhook, officially called the Fulton Surface-to-Air Recovery System (STARS), was tested, approved, and used in real missions during the Cold War. A person on the ground wears a harness which is connected by a nylon cable to a giant balloon hanging in the sky. The MC-130E plane flies into the cable, the V-shaped fork catches it, and the person on the ground shoots into the sky. The plane's crew then opens the rear cargo bay door and retrieves the person dangling using a winch.

## Historical Use

The CIA used this technology operationally in 1962 as part of Operation COLDFEET in which personnel were extracted from the ground after investigating an abandoned Soviet research station in the Arctic. One of its most famous real uses was during the Vietnam War, when U.S. forces used it to recover agents and even equipment from enemy territory.

## Development
The Fulton surface-to-air recovery system was developed by inventor Robert Edison Fulton, Jr., for the CIA in the early 1950s. Experiments with the recovery system began in 1950 by the CIA and Air Force, using a weather balloon, nylon line, and weights of 10 to 15 pounds.

## First Successful Use
The first human pickup using Fulton's STARS took place on 12 August 1958, when Staff Sergeant Levi W. Woods of the U.S. Marine Corps was winched on board the Neptune.

## Early Operational Use
However, there was an earlier operational attempt: The first human recovery mission authorized for operational use of this "all American system" took place in Manchuria on 29 November 1952. The first reported operational use of STARS was Operation COLDFEET, a covert mission conducted by the CIA and the US Navy in 1962.

## System Decommissioning
In September 1996, the Air Force Special Operations Command ceased maintaining the capability to deploy this system.

The Principality of Sealand is a micronation on HM Fort Roughs (also known as Roughs Tower), an offshore platform in the North Sea located approximately 11 kilometres from the coast of Suffolk and 13 kilometres from the coast of Essex.

Roughs Tower is a Maunsell Sea Fort that was built by the British in international waters during World War II. Since 1967, the decommissioned Roughs Tower has been occupied and claimed as a sovereign state by the family and associates of Paddy Roy Bates.

Bates seized Roughs Tower from a group of pirate radio broadcasters in 1967 with the intention of setting up his own station there. ## Recording Details

Victor 20964-A was recorded on September 14, 1927 and was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1978. In 1928, "My Blue Heaven" became a huge hit on Victor 20964-A for crooner Gene Austin, accompanied by the Victor Orchestra as directed by Nat Shilkret.

## Sales Figures

It charted for 26 weeks, stayed at number one for 13, and sold over five million copies worldwide. However, there are varying sales claims - Gene Austin's My Blue Heaven eventually sold 12 million copies, making it one of the most successful singles of all time.

## Historical Significance

Until Bing Crosby's "White Christmas" replaced it, it was the largest selling record of all time. The February 22, 1928 issue of Variety had reported, "The biggest selling popular vocal artist on all records now is Gene Austin, exclusive Victor artist whose Forgive Me recording went over 500,000 disks and My Blue Heaven will exceed that."

The recording featured a minimal arrangement with piano and cello, and notably included bird calls as a vocal novelty element.

## The First Solo Woman to Thru-Hike the Appalachian Trail

Emma "Grandma" Gatewood was the first woman to solo thru-hike the Appalachian Trail. When she summited Katahdin on September 25, 1955, she became the first woman ever to complete the entire A.T. alone in one season.

### Key Details About Her Achievement

She was 67 years old at the time, a mother of 11, a grandmother of 23, and a survivor of more than 30 years of domestic abuse. Emma walked for 146 days, through 14 states, took 5 million steps, lost 30 pounds, went through 7 pairs of shoes, and gained and lost altitude on the trail the equivalent of climbing Mt. Everest 16 times all at age 67.

### Her Remarkable Minimalist Approach

Gatewood hiked the trail carrying a homemade knapsack and wearing ordinary sneakers — she wore out six pairs of them in 146 days from May to September. She brought a blanket and a plastic shower curtain to protect her from the elements, but she didn't bother with a sleeping bag, a tent, a compass or even a map, instead relying on the hospitality of strangers along the way and her own independent resourcefulness.

### Her Legacy

Many women, after hearing about Gatewood's trek, convinced themselves that if Grandma Gatewood could hike the Appalachian Trail, so could they. In the years since Gatewood's accomplishment, the A.T. has increasingly become more inclusive of women.

On October 31, 1950, 21-year-old Earl Lloyd becomes the first African American to play in an NBA game when he takes the court in the season opener for the Washington Capitols.

However, it's important to note that while Lloyd was the first to actually play in an NBA game, Chuck Cooper made history when he became the first African-American player to be drafted by an NBA team on April 25, 1950, and Nat Clifton became the first Black player to sign a contract in the NBA in 1950.

Two other Black players joined the NBA that season—the Celtics drafted Chuck Cooper in the second round and the New York Knicks got Nat "Sweetwater" Clifton from the Harlem Globetrotters—but the Knicks and the Celts didn't start their seasons until November. As a result, Lloyd became a coincidental pioneer: the first Black player to make his debut in the NBA.

Reichsmarschall was an honorary military rank, specially created for Hermann Göring during World War II, and the de jure highest rank in the Wehrmacht. The rank was equivalent to Generalfeldmarschall, a five-star rank comparable to OF-10 in today's NATO naval forces.

## Director and Development Team

Ocarina of Time was led by five directors, including Eiji Aonuma and Yoshiaki Koizumi, and produced by series co-creator Shigeru Miyamoto.

## Development Process

Development of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time commenced in Late 1994 during the same time when Nintendo was developing Super Mario 64, and they presented the game originally at the Nintendo Space World of 1995 in December.

Shigeru Miyamoto gave the rights to direct Ocarina of Time to various people, each focusing on various points of the game. However, things went awry under the direction of the multiple designers, and thus Miyamoto stepped in to straighten things out.

## Legacy of the Directors

All of the directors of the game, especially Eiji Aonuma and Yoshiaki Koizumi, went on to become prominent figures at Nintendo, the two spearheading the way for the Zelda and Mario franchise, respectively.
