## Location and Basic Facts

Syros is a Greek island in the Cyclades, in the Aegean Sea. It is 78 nautical miles (144 km) south-east of Athens. The area of the island is 83.6 km² (32 sq mi) and at the 2021 census it had 21,124 inhabitants.

## Capital Status

As the capital of the Cyclades, Syros is an island that blends elegance, culture and everyday life befitting its status as the administrative centre of Greece's most iconic island group. Ermoupoli is the capital of the island, the Cyclades, and the South Aegean.

## Main Towns and Architecture

Its main town, Ermoupoli, spreads amphitheatrically above the harbour and is filled with grand squares and neoclassical mansions that recall its 19th-century status as a major shipping and trading hub. Above Ermoupoli, Ano Syros is a labyrinth of whitewashed alleys, vaulted passages and Venetian charm, crowned by the Catholic Cathedral of Agios Georgios.

## Historical Significance

The history of settlement on Syros goes back at least 5,000 years, to the Early Bronze Age of the Cycladic civilization. This is when the hill-top settlement of Kastri began.

## Accessibility

Syros is one of the most accessible islands in the Cyclades, with regular connections by both air and sea. Syros has a small domestic airport with year-round flights from Athens and seasonal flights from Thessaloniki. The flight takes around 35-40 minutes from Athens.

As a 23-year-old soda fountain worker, Strickler liked testing new ice cream combinations to attract customers, and his idea of slicing a banana lengthwise and topping it with scoops of vanilla, chocolate, and strawberry ice cream quickly became popular with local students at nearby Saint Vincent College. Based on the search results, here's the information about the Eagle Awards comics co-founders and history:

## Co-Founders

The Eagle Awards were set up by prominent British comics enthusiasts Mike Conroy, Nick Landau, Colin Campbell, Phil Clarke, and Richard Burton.

## Origins and 1977 Launch

Because the Eagle logo was perceived as "a standard of quality ... seldom reached" in early 1977, the Eagle Awards were named "with official blessing from IPC" (Eagle's former publisher). 

Named after the UK's seminal boys' comic Eagle, the awards were launched in 1977 for comics released in 1976. The first awards ceremony was held on 3 September 1977 at the Bloomsbury Centre Hotel, London.

## Purpose and Impact

The awards were "set up and financed by a group of dealers and fanzine editors" with the intention of including "people with... diverse interests... to make the poll as impartial as possible," and were described as "the first independent [in the UK], nationally organised comic art awards poll."

The hope was that the Eagle Awards would "become a regular annual fandom event," and indeed, they were the preeminent British comics award in the 1980s and the 2000s.

## Overview
Komodo National Park, located in the center of the Indonesian archipelago, between the islands of Sumbawa and Flores, is composed of three major islands (Rinca, Komodo, and Padar) and numerous smaller ones, all of them of volcanic origin.

## UNESCO Recognition
In 1991 the national park was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a Man and Biosphere Reserve.

## Islands and Size
The park includes the three larger islands Komodo, Padar and Rinca, and 26 smaller ones, with a total area of 1,733 km2 (669 sq mi), with 603 km2 (233 sq mi) of it land.

## Primary Purpose
The national park was founded in 1980 to protect the Komodo dragon, the world's largest lizard. These volcanic islands are inhabited by a population of around 5,700 giant lizards, whose appearance and aggressive behaviour have led to them being called 'Komodo dragons'. They exist nowhere else in the world and are of great interest to scientists studying the theory of evolution.

## Biodiversity
Located at the juncture of two continental plates, this national park constitutes the "shatter belt" within the Wallacea Biogeographical Region, between the Australian and Sunda ecosystems. The property is identified as a global conservation priority area, comprising unparalleled terrestrial and marine ecosystems and covers a total area of 219,322 ha.

## Rotation and Liftoff Pitch Angles

Aircraft typically lift off at a nose-up pitch of around 10 degrees during normal takeoff operations. However, the pitch angles can vary depending on the specific technique used:

**Semi-Rotation Technique:**
Early in the takeoff roll, you can rotate to a pitch attitude of 3 degrees or so, which helps manage runway irregularities.

**Standard Rotation:**
Part way down the runway you rotate so that the pitch attitude is about 7.5 degrees, and the plane lifts off when it has enough airspeed to support its weight at a 12 degree angle of attack.

**General Aircraft Design Limits:**
In most aircraft the aft-body and/or tail bumper is designed such that the aircraft cannot rotate by more than a specified number of degrees at liftoff, typically between 12 and 15 degrees.

## Light Aircraft Specific Information

In a Cessna or Piper, the pilot applies back pressure on the yoke or stick, the nose pitches up, and the aircraft lifts off at the appropriate airspeed found in the aircraft's operating handbook, which varies with weight and conditions.

Based on the document, the specific pitch angle depends on the takeoff procedure being used:

**Normal Takeoff:** The aircraft rotates to approximately **7.5 degrees** pitch attitude at rotation, which corresponds to a 12-degree angle of attack.

**Soft-Field Takeoff:** The nose rises to roughly **15 degrees** pitch attitude, approaching the stalling angle of attack, then gradually lowers to maintain altitude just above the ground.

**Obstructed-Field Takeoff:** The rotation reaches approximately **15.5 degrees** pitch attitude to achieve maximum climb gradient over obstacles.

## Alfred A. Knopf

Alfred attended Columbia University, where he was a pre-law student and a member of the Peithologian Society (a debating and literary club) and the Boar's Head Society. ## Blanche Knopf

Unlike Alfred, Blanche Knopf did not attend a traditional university. Educated at home by French and German governesses and at the Gardner School in New York, Blanche became fluent in several languages, especially French, which she spoke as if it were her native tongue. Informed in part by Alfred's professors at Columbia University and Blanche's education at the Gardner School for Girls, the Knopfs initially emphasized European writers on their lists.

## Founding the Publishing House

Knopf, along with Blanche Knopf, founded the publishing house Alfred A. Knopf in 1915.

## Original Name and Founding

Columbia University was officially founded on October 31, 1754, as King's College by royal charter of King George II, making it the oldest institution of higher learning in the state of New York and the fifth oldest in the United States. The College was established by a royal charter issued by Great Britain's King George II, and the College's first president, Samuel Johnson, presided over its first-ever class, which was held in a schoolhouse connected to Trinity Church in lower Manhattan.

## Name Changes

The institution went through several name changes reflecting major historical events:

**After the American Revolution**: It was renamed Columbia College when it reopened in 1784 after the American Revolution. "Columbia" was a poetic or symbolic name for the United States in the 1700s and 1800s, and in 1784, after independence, it was renamed Columbia College to honor the new nation.

**Becoming a University**: It became Columbia University in 1912. However, other sources indicate in 1896, Columbia College in the City of New York was renamed Columbia University in the City of New York, with the undergraduate school retaining the name Columbia College.

The NES CPU was a custom Ricoh chip (RP2A03 for NTSC and RP2A07 for PAL regions) based on the MOS Technology 6502 processor used in the Apple II.

The NES employed a modified 6502 CPU, an admired ingredient of late-70s and early-80s computers. More specifically, the MOS 6502 CPU was used in several famous early computers, including the Apple II and the Commodore PET.

The connection between the NES processor and Apple goes even further: Nintendo opted for the WDC 65C816, a 16-bit extension of the 6502, which was found on the Apple IIGS for the Super Nintendo.

## Founding and First Issue

The Atlantic Monthly was founded by Moses Dresser Phillips and Francis H. Underwood in Boston in 1857. The first issue of the magazine was published on November 1, 1857.

## History and Purpose

It was founded in 1857 in Boston as The Atlantic Monthly, a literary and cultural magazine that published leading writers' commentary on education, the abolition of slavery, and other major political issues of that time. James Russell Lowell was its first editor.

## First Issue Content

That first issue included Emerson's "Days" and "Brahma," works by Whittier and Longfellow, and Lowell's satire on didactic verse. Three short stories and the first installment of a serial novel occupied about a third of the magazine's 128 pages, and all reflected the New England local color realism that was to characterize much Atlantic fiction.

## Legacy

It is one of the nation's most venerable and respected publications. From its founding in 1857 until its sale by Houghton Mifflin in 1908, the Atlantic Monthly was the most respected literary periodical in the United States.

## Founded in 1881

The Century Magazine was an illustrated monthly magazine first published in the United States in 1881 by The Century Company of New York City, which had been bought in that year by Roswell Smith and renamed by him after the Century Association.

## Background and History

It was the successor of Scribner's Monthly Magazine. The initial editor was to have been Scribner's editor and co-owner Josiah G. Holland, but he died prior to the appearance of the first issue. He was succeeded by Richard Watson Gilder, the managing editor of Scribner's, who would go on to helm The Century for 28 years.

## Early Success and Notable Content

These institutional changes and Gilder's keen editorial guidance resulted in prosperity during the 1880s, when the Century expanded from a circulation of about 125,000 in 1881 to a peak of 250,000 by the middle of the decade.

The magazine was very successful during the 19th century, most notably for a series of articles about the American Civil War which ran for three years during the 1880s.

## Later History

In 1929, due to competition from cheaper magazines and newspapers, The Century became a quarterly, and in 1930 it was merged with The Forum.

## Location and Overview

God's Window is nestled in the Blyde River Canyon Nature Reserve, located in the Mpumalanga province of South Africa. It sits along the Drakensberg escarpment at an altitude of approximately 1,829 meters (6,000 feet) above sea level.

## The Name

The attraction's name comes from its breathtaking view, with vast views from a significant height that sometimes sees clouds at the same level, which prompts many to consider the view something you could only see from the 'heavens'.

## Views and Scenic Features

God's Window is so called for the panoramic view of the Lowveld more than 900 m down into lush indigenous forest clad ravine. This elevated position provides an uninterrupted view over the Lowveld, where on a clear day, visitors can see as far as the Kruger National Park and even Mozambique.

## Activities and Attractions

The attraction is in the Blyde River Canyon Nature Reserve, which offers plenty of things to see and do, from hiking to bird watching and other exciting outdoor activities. The 2024 fees are R25 per adult and R15 per child.

The area is part of the Panorama Route, a roughly 160 km route in Mpumalanga, that runs between Lydenburg and the border of Mpumalanga and Limpopo near the Echo Caves.

## Origin and Name

Prinsjesdag (Prince's Day) was originally the name given to 8 March, the birthday of Stadholder William V (1748-1806). In an era marked by political divisions between supporters and opponents of the House of Orange, Prinsjesdag was one of the country's most popular holidays. During the French occupation, supporters of the House of Orange-Nassau demonstrated their loyalty to the prince by continuing to celebrate this day.

## When the Name Was Applied to Parliament Opening

The current name was chosen in the 19th century for the ceremonial opening of parliament. In the 19th century, Prinsjesdag was given the function that it has today: The head of state reads out the governmental plans. However, no one really knows why, many years later, the name Prinsjesdag was given to the day on which Parliament opens.

## Modern Date and Schedule

Article 65 of the Constitution states that a statement of the policy to be pursued by the Government shall be given before a joint session of the two Houses of the States-General every year on the third Tuesday in September. In 1887 Budget Day was moved to the third Tuesday in September, where it has remained ever since.

## Official Distance

The infield shall be a 90-foot square. This means the distance between bases in baseball is 90 feet.

## How It's Measured

The measurement process is specific: When the location of home base is determined, use a steel tape measure of 127 feet, 3 3/8 inches in the desired direction to establish second base. The distance between first base and third base is 127 feet, 3 3/8 inches.

An important detail to understand: The 90 feet is measured to the back of the bases. When you measure the straight line distance between the two closest points between two bases, it's about 88 feet.

## Historical Context

During a convention of baseball clubs in 1857, it was proposed to standardize the distance between bases at 90 feet, which was adopted by the National Association of Base Ball Players (NABP) in 1859.

These measurements apply to professional Major League Baseball and have remained consistent for over 160 years.

## Technicolor Dye-Transfer Process

Technicolor Process 3 (1928) was developed based on the dye-transfer technique first applied to motion pictures in 1916 by Max Handschiegl. Cyan, yellow, and magenta dyes were added one at a time by pressing a dyed matrix, or relief film, into contact with the blank for a short time.

The dye-transfer printing process was introduced for two-color printing in 1926, adapted for three-color in the 1930s and remained in use in the United States until the mid-1970s. The closure of Technicolor's Hollywood laboratory in 1975 marked the demise of dye-transfer printing in the United States, followed by the British laboratory in 1978 and the Italian in 1980, with The Godfather Part II (1974) among the last films to be printed in dye-transfer.

## Capital Status in 1799

In 1799, Philadelphia was the US capital city, having become capital by 1792 and remaining the capital for ten years.

## The Move to Washington DC

The Residence Act of July 16, 1790, established the nation's capital in current-day Washington. However, the capital moved back to Philadelphia for 10 years until the new capital was built on the Potomac.

Congress ended its business in Philadelphia on May 15, 1800, and Philadelphia ceased to officially be the nation's capital on June 11, 1800. President Adams left Philadelphia in April 1800 and moved into the White House in November.

## Why the Change

The Residence Act put the nation's capital in Washington as part of a plan to appease pro-slavery states who feared a northern capital as being too sympathetic to abolitionists.

## Salonica (Thessaloniki)

The primary city associated with this epithet is Salonica — an Aegean port situated at the crossroads of Europe and the Middle East — was once home to the world's largest Sephardic Jewish community. The image of the 16th-century golden age of Salonica as a center of Jewish refuge and Jewish learning is conjured by the expression, "the Jerusalem of the Balkans."

The Jewish community blossomed in the 16th century, when Salonica became a major refuge for Jews exiled from Spain and Portugal. By the mid-16th century, Jews constituted half of the city's residents and formed one of the largest Jewish communities in the early modern world.

Based on the search results, here's information about the Victory Salute statue in San Jose, California:

## Overview

Victory Salute, commonly referred to as the Olympic Black Power Statue, is a monument depicting the 1968 Olympics Black Power salute performed by African-American athletes Tommie Smith and John Carlos. In 2005, San Jose State University honored former students Smith and Carlos with a 22-foot-high statue of their protest titled Victory Salute, created by artist Rigo 23.

## Historical Context

During the medal ceremony for the 200-meter running final in the Olympic Stadium in Mexico City on October 16, 1968, the athletes performed the Black power salute, raising their fists in silent protest. Smith, in the first place spot and Carlos, in third, planned and executed the gesture to draw attention to injustice and inequality faced by Black Americans but were greeted with boos and threats from the audience.

## Design and Location

Rigo 23, a Portuguese-born artist often associated with the Black Power and equal rights movements, constructed the piece in the center of the San Jose State University campus. The statues were constructed from fiberglass over steel supports and covered with ceramic tiles, their track pants and jackets form a mosaic of dark blue ceramic tiles, with red and white detailing on the stripes of the track suits.

## Unique Feature

Peter Norman asked to be excluded from the monument, so that visitors could participate by standing in his place, and feeling what he felt. There is a plaque in the empty spot which reads "Fellow Athlete Australian Peter Norman Stood Here in Solidarity; Take a Stand".

Based on the search results, here's what I found about the Philippines' first Winter Olympics participation:

## Philippines' Winter Games Debut

The Philippines made its Winter Games debut at Sapporo 1972 in Japan with Alpine skiers, Juan Cipriano and Ben Nanasca, taking to the hill, and the nation has competed in several editions since.

## Historical Significance

Not only was this the Philippines' first-ever appearance at the quadrennial event, but it also marked the first time in history for a tropical country to be represented in the Olympic Winter Games. What made this even more remarkable was the fact that the Philippines was years ahead of other Southeast Asian nations. With tropical climates ruling the region, it took decades for neighboring countries to achieve the same feat; Thailand made its first appearance in 2002, while Malaysia and Singapore debuted in 2018.

## The Athletes

Ben and Juan were cousins who grew up in the Philippines before being adopted as teenagers by a New Zealand family. Their journey took them across Europe—Andorra, Spain, France, and Switzerland—where they trained extensively in alpine skiing.

## Subsequent Appearances

The South East Asian nation the Philippines, composed of 7,007 islands, first competed at the Winter Olympic Games in 1972, fielding a couple of alpine skiers. The nation then showed up in three more editions of the Winter Games in 1988, 1992 and 2014.

## Overview

The Volkswagen Scirocco is a three-door, front-engine, front-wheel-drive, sport compact hatchback manufactured and marketed by Volkswagen in two generations from 1974 to 1992 and a third generation from 2008 until 2017.

## First Generation (1974-1981)

Volkswagen began work on the car during the early 1970s as the replacement for the aging Karmann Ghia coupe, and designated it the Typ 53 internally. The Scirocco debuted at the 1973 Geneva Motor Show and went on sale in Europe in 1974 and in North America in 1975. Up to 1981, more than 500,000 units of the Scirocco I were sold throughout the world.

## Second Generation (1981-1992)

The Scirocco II was launched in 1981 with an elongated wedge-shaped body, softer lines and a rear spoiler installed above the rear window. Production of the Scirocco II, assembled by Karmann in Osnabrück, came to an end on September 7, 1992 after 291,497 units.

## Third Generation (2008-2017)

Volkswagen officially announced in June 2006 production of a new Scirocco model at the AutoEuropa assembly plant in Palmela, Portugal. The new model, identified by the internal type numbers 137 or 1K8, is based on the PQ35 platform of the Golf V and was unveiled at the 2008 Geneva Motor Show. It went on sale in summer 2008 in Europe, with sales in other countries beginning early 2009.

## The Mossi People

The Mossi are a Gur ethnic group native to modern Burkina Faso, primarily the Volta River basin, and constitute the largest ethnic group in Burkina Faso, making up 52% of the population or about 11.1 million people.

## The Moore Language

The Mossi speak the Mooré language, of the Western Oti-Volta group of languages, northwestern sub-group. It is spoken in Burkina Faso, Ghana, and Ivory Coast.

Mooré is a Gur language of the Oti–Volta branch and one of the three official languages of Burkina Faso. It is spoken by approximately 6.46 million people in Burkina Faso, Ghana, Ivory Coast, Benin, Niger, Mali, Togo, and Senegal as a native language.

## Language Characteristics

There are a few dialects based mainly on region, for example in Yatenga, the northern region, Koupela in the southeast, and Tenkodogo, and despite these regional differences, the dialects are mutually intelligible. Moore is a tonal language and is one of the official languages of Burkina Faso.

California voted for the Republican nominee, Vice President Richard Nixon, over the Democratic nominee, Massachusetts Senator John F. Kennedy. However, this was a very close race. Nixon's margin of victory over Kennedy turned out to be extremely narrow; in fact, it was the closest of the states that Nixon won, and the fourth closest state in the election after Hawaii, Illinois and Missouri.

Interestingly, on the morning of November 9, the NBC victory desk erroneously projected California for Kennedy, but a count of absentee ballots gave Nixon the state several weeks later, after he conceded it to Kennedy.

So while Kennedy won the 1960 presidential election overall, Nixon won California, though by an extremely narrow margin in his home state.

## Ethel Sands' Life Partner

Ethel Sands met fellow student Nan Hudson, born Anna Hope Hudson in the United States, who became her life partner. Ethel Sands met her partner, artist Anna Hope Hudson (known as Nan), when she was just 23 years old, and the pair met in Paris in 1893. Walter Sickert created multiple works featuring Ethel Sands:

3. **Portrait of Ethel Sands** (1913-14): This is a portrait of Ethel Sands by Walter Richard Sickert.

The friendship between Walter Richard Sickert and the American painters Ethel Sands and Nan Hudson lasted for over twenty years and led to the two women's inclusion in the Fitzroy Street Group and subsequently the London Group.

## Cancer

The breed records higher levels of cancer than other breeds, which stands out as particularly significant. It is estimated that 56% of female and 66% of male Goldens will die as a result of some form of malignancy. Hemangiosarcoma is an aggressive and fast-growing form of cancer seen in dogs overall and in Goldens in particular, with other forms including Lymphosarcoma, Osteosarcoma, and Mastocytoma.

## Hip and Elbow Dysplasia

Golden Retrievers experience higher than average levels of hip dysplasia and joint issues such as canine arthritis. Hip and elbow dysplasia are two of the most common Golden Retriever health issues.

## Allergies

More than many other breeds, Golden Retrievers are prone to allergies, which can cause skin problems like lick granulomas or hot spots, with wheat allergies being common in this breed, as are environmental allergies.

## Ear Infections

Due to their floppy ears, Golden Retrievers can be more prone to ear infections than other dog breeds, especially if their ears aren't kept clean, dry, and groomed.

## Other Conditions

Similar to other large breeds, Goldens have health risks concerning their heart, lungs, and circulation, with a common condition being subvalvular aortic stenosis (SAS), when the aorta starts to narrow.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about the connection between mustard gas and chemotherapy development:

## Historical Connection

The development of modern chemotherapy has its roots in chemical warfare, specifically in the use of mustard gas during World War I. Edward Bell Krumbhaar, a medical officer with American forces in France, studied the effects of mustard gas on soldiers and noted its tendency to kill bone marrow and suppress white blood cell production. However, in 1943, an air raid of a ship carrying mustard gas during World War II resulted in mustard gas poisoning of survivors, and upon noticing leukopenia in these patients, the first chemotherapy for leukemia using nitrogen mustard was born.

## Nitrogen Mustard Development

By replacing the sulfur atom with a nitrogen atom in sulfur mustard, nitrogen mustard (now called mechlorethamine) was formed. Experiments with transplanted lymphosarcomas in mice confirmed the cytotoxic action of mechlorethamine on lymphoid tissue, and the first clinical trials in 1943 marked the dawn of modern cancer chemotherapy.

## Mechanism of Action

Nitrogen mustard works by damaging the DNA of rapidly dividing cancer cells, thereby inhibiting their growth.

## Modern Applications

Nitrogen mustard and its derivatives have been used in the treatment of several cancers, including malignant melanomas, lymphomas, and others. Drugs such as cyclophosphamide and chlorambucil are still used today, demonstrating the lasting legacy of early research into mustard gas.

Mustard gas or sulfur mustard are names commonly used for the organosulfur chemical compound bis(2-chloroethyl) sulfide.

Alternative names include: Distilled mustard, 2,2'-Dichlorodiethyl sulfide, Di(2-chloroethyl) sulfide, Dichlorodiethyl sulfide, and Dichloroethyl sulfide.

Sulfur mustard has been referred to by a number of synonyms: S-mustard, to distinguish it from nitrogen mustard; "Lost" or "S-Lost," from the names of two chemists who suggested it be used as a war gas (Lommel and Steinkopf); "yellow cross," for the identifying mark on WWI shells containing sulfur mustard; or Yperite, after the site of its first use in 1917.

## The Event

On September 30, 1962, riots erupted on the campus of the University of Mississippi in Oxford where locals, students, and committed segregationists had gathered to protest the enrollment of James Meredith, a black Air Force veteran attempting to integrate the all-white school.

## The Casualties

When the smoke cleared the following morning, two civilians were dead and scores more were reported injured. More specifically, there were two people dead and 166 wounded. Seventy-nine of the 127 Marshals Service personnel were wounded.

## Context and Legal Battle

Meredith, an African American who had served in the Air Force and completed coursework at Jackson State University, selected Ole Miss as it was a symbol of "white prestige and power" attended by the children of the state's elite. On September 10, 1962, Justice Hugo Black delivered the court's decision: Meredith must be admitted for the fall semester.

## Federal Response

President John F. Kennedy eventually quelled the riot by mobilizing more than 30,000 troops, the most for a single disturbance in United States history.

## Successful Enrollment

The day after the riots, on October 1, 1962, after federal and state forces took control, Meredith became the first African-American student to enroll at the University of Mississippi.

Clonidine was patented in 1961 and came into medical use in 1966. At the beginning of the 1960s Boehringer Ingelheim planned to synthesize a peripherally active adrenergic compound for nasal decongestion as simple nose drops.

Although the resulting drug indeed had a remarkably high vasoconstructive and decongestive effect at low concentrations, it turned out that other effects were more significant. After the first trial in humans, it became clear that clonidine's decongestant properties were far less interesting than its potent anti-hypertensive effects. The compound was then developed for this new indication and was introduced into therapy in 1966 under the trade name Catapres.

The primary patent expirations for the original clonidine hydrochloride occurred in the 1980s.

The Bird Girl statue, designed both as art and as a birdseed holder, was originally located in Bonaventure Cemetery, and a Savannah photographer, Jack Leigh, was commissioned to take a photograph for the cover of the book.

Photographer Jack Leigh's 1993 image titled "Midnight" depicts a grave monument in Bonaventure cemetery featuring a bronze statue of a slender girl in a full length dress, holding a pair of bowls in outstretched arms. The statue is one of four, originally cast in 1936 by sculptor Sylvia Shaw Judson.

The cover image became immediately iconic, with author John Berendt calling it "one of the strongest covers I've ever seen", and the statue became a popular stop for tourists. However, owing to rising concerns about the integrity of the statue and the cemetery's privacy, Bird Girl was relocated in 1997 for display in Telfair Museums in Savannah.

The success was remarkable: Two years after the book's release, Savannah was seeing a 46% increase in tourism. Twenty years later, the number of visitors to the city had jumped to 12.5 million, spending $2.2 billion.

## Search Results Summary

Here's what the web search found about epidemic victims buried in Colonial Park Cemetery in downtown Savannah, GA:

### Overview
Colonial Park Cemetery is an 18th- and early 19th-century burial ground located in downtown Savannah, Georgia. The cemetery was established in 1750, when Savannah was the capital of the British Province of Georgia, last of the Thirteen Colonies.

### Yellow Fever Epidemic of 1820
Nearly 700 Savannahians died during the Great Yellow Fever Epidemic of 1820, including two local physicians who lost their lives caring for the stricken. At the northern end of Colonial Park Cemetery is a mass grave that holds almost 700 bodies of people who died during the Yellow Fever epidemic of 1820.

In a desperate response to the sheer number of deaths, a mass grave was dug within the cemetery's grounds to accommodate the many victims. While historical records suggest that nearly 700 people were interred in this mass burial, oral histories and legends hint that the true number might have been significantly higher.

### Cemetery Significance
Covering 6 acres, it holds over 9,000 graves, many unmarked due to hasty epidemic burials and erosion over time. It became a city park in 1896, 43 years after burials in the cemetery ceased, and is open to visitors.

Based on the search results, here are the surviving buildings from the World's Columbian Exposition of 1893:

## Buildings Still Standing on the Fairgrounds

The Palace of Fine Arts in Chicago is the only original building to still be standing on the fair's grounds. This Beaux Arts domed building now serves as the Museum of Science and Industry at 5700 S. Lake Shore Dr. The Palace of Fine Arts was built with brick and steel because many nations wouldn't allow their art to be displayed in a non-fireproof building.

The Art Institute of Chicago building is the second of the two remaining buildings from the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition.

## Relocated Structures

Several other significant buildings from the fair still exist but have been relocated:

- **Norway Building**: The Norway Building was a recreation of a traditional wooden stave church. After the Fair it was relocated to Lake Geneva, and in 1935 was moved to a museum called Little Norway in Blue Mounds, Wisconsin. In 2015 it was dismantled and shipped back to Norway, where it was restored and reassembled.

- **Maine State Building**: The Maine State Building, designed by Charles Sumner Frost, was purchased by the Ricker family of Poland Spring, Maine. They moved the building to their resort to serve as a library and art gallery. The Poland Spring Preservation Society now owns the building, which was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1974.

- **Dutch House**: The Dutch House was moved to Brookline, Massachusetts. It was placed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1986.

Additionally, a restroom building from the fair stands just behind the south side of the Museum of Science and Industry.

## Key Findings:

**Natural Host and Carrier Species:**
Herpes B virus (also known as monkey B virus) is carried by several species of macaque monkeys, which are thought to be a "natural host" for the virus.

**Large Populations in China and Florida:**

*China:* China has a large number of macaques, which is the backbone of scientific research in non-human primates. Additionally, the first case of human infection with herpes B virus was recently reported in China - a 53-year-old veterinarian who specialized in breeding and experimental research of nonhuman primates in a research institute in Beijing.

*Florida:* About 175 free-roaming rhesus macaques inhabit Silver Springs State Park, descended from a population of around a dozen animals that were released in the 1930s to promote local tourism. About 25 percent of the monkeys carry macacine herpesvirus 1 (McHV-1), which causes only mild symptoms, if any, in monkeys but can be deadly in people.

Herpes B virus infection can be fatal to humans, with a mortality rate as high as 70–80% without timely treatment.

## Key Information

Advanced Cell Technology, Inc. (ACT) was formed in 1994 and grew from a small agricultural cloning research facility located in Worcester, Massachusetts, into a multi-locational corporation involved in stem cell technology.

Michael West, a biotechnology entrepreneur, was appointed president and CEO of ACT in 1998.

### Endangered Species Cloning

Through its specialty in cross species nuclear transplantation, ACT participated in a collaborative effort to clone, for the first time, an endangered species animal, which culminated in the birth of a gaur named Noah in 2001. The researchers used cryopreserved gaur skin cells combined with an embryo of a domestic cow, and a domestic cow also served as the surrogate for the developing gaur clone.

However, Noah was born on 8 January 2001, but died two days later due to dysentery. Cloning of other endangered species proved unsuccessful.

### Michael West's Role

In the late 1990s, Advanced Cell Technology's then Chief Executive Officer and President Michael West recognized a link between the current extinctions and assisted reproduction technologies. West also led the company's expansion into human embryonic stem cell research and therapeutic cloning, which became highly controversial.

On September 14 [O.S. 4 September] 1607, Irish earls Hugh O'Neill, Earl of Tyrone, and Rory O'Donnell, Earl of Tyrconnell, permanently departed Rathmullan in Ireland for Catholic Europe during a period of extreme political tension with the English Crown.

Meehan was responsible for popularising the term "Flight of the Earls", since he titled Ó Cianáin's manuscript The Narrative of the Flight of the Earls. Charles Patrick Meehan's 1868 book The fate and fortunes of Hugh O'Neill, earl of Tyrone, and Rory O'Donel, earl of Tyrconnel was a major study on the motivations and effects of the Flight.

More specifically, Meehan was responsible for popularising the term 'flight of the earls' by his extensive use of a contemporary manuscript by Tadhg Ó Cianáin, and the untitled manuscript was called by Meehan 'the narrative of the Flight of the Earls'. When the manuscript's first full translation by Father Paul Walsh appeared in 1913-4, it appeared under the title The Flight of the Earls, due to the influence of Fate and Fortunes.

So while the historical event occurred in 1607, the terminology "Flight of the Earls" was popularized by Meehan's 1868 book, which was the first to use this phrase when he titled Ó Cianáin's manuscript account.

## Slush Puppie's Name Origin

Slush Puppie founder Will Radcliff decided to start the company after seeing a slush-making machine at a Chicago trade fair in 1970, and Radcliff, his sister and their mother came up with the name "Slush Puppie" based on hush puppy.

## Hushpuppy Connection

The name "Slush Puppie" is a playful reference to hushpuppies, a cornmeal-based food with Southern roots. Hushpuppies are rounds of deep-fried cornmeal batter, crisp on the outside, warm and soft on the inside with a rich, toasty corn flavor.

## Hushpuppy Origin

Regarding hushpuppies themselves, they were originally called red horse bread, named after the red horse fish of the South Carolina rivers. "Red horse bread" is associated with formerly enslaved chef Romeo Govan and said to have been similar in consistency and ingredients, and "Red horse bread" of South Carolina then became "hushpuppies" in Georgia around 1927, then gained national traction around 1943 in Florida.

The exact origin of the "hushpuppy" name itself remains unclear, though the name has no verified origin.

The Canadian Museum of History is one of Canada's oldest public institutions, with roots stretching back to 1856. More specifically, in 1856, Sir William Edmond Logan, the first director of the Geological Survey of Canada (GSC), opened a public museum in Montréal with the support of an act passed by the Province of Canada.

In 1986, it was renamed the Canadian Museum of Civilization, and opened to the public in 1989 in its current location in Gatineau. On 12 December 2013, the Museum of Civilization was renamed the Canadian Museum of History.

So while the institution was founded in **1856**, it became known as the Canadian Museum of History specifically in 2013.

## Gamsonite: The "Pseudo-Label"

Cook created Gamsonite, a "pseudo-label" collecting his early collaborations. More specifically, in 2012, Cook launched Gamsonite, a short-lived Tumblr-based "pseudo-label" described as an unfinished research project into personal computer music, where he uploaded early experimental tracks and collaborations with emerging artists like GFOTY and Kero Kero Bonito.

## Context and Purpose

This platform marked Cook's initial foray into the DIY electronic scene, distributing remixes and originals via free downloads to build a niche online audience. He's described Gamsonite as "a prototype for PC Music", the influential record label he would go on to found in 2013.

## Connection to Other Early Projects

Gamsonite was part of Cook's broader experimental work during this period. After studying music in the University of London, A.G. Cook began collaborating with friends with similar tastes on electronic music, combining avant-garde experimentation with tongue-in-cheek surreal humor, leading to the formation of projects including Dux Content with longtime friend/producer Danny L. Harle, and a "pseudo-label" of collaborations known as Gamsonite.

## Key Information

Paul-Albert Bartholomé was a French painter and sculptor who was born on 29 August 1848 in Thiverval-Grignon, Yvelines, France, and died in 1928 in Paris. He won the Grand Prize for sculpture at the Exposition Universelle in 1900.

## Major War Monuments

Bartholomé's masterpiece is the monument in Père Lachaise Cemetery dedicated to all the dead, which he worked on for ten years with the inauguration taking place in 1899. The "Monument the Dead" involves twenty-one larger-than-life-size figures all showing different emotions and reactions to death.

Regarding his 1919-related work, sculptor Albert Bartholomé designed the croix de guerre in 1915 for a French military medal commending acts of exceptional valor. Additionally, French president Raymond Poincaré originally charged Bartholomé with the Monument aux Américains project at the Pointe de la Grave, though in 1922 Bourdelle and Ventre joined the design team.

# Bartholomé's War Memorials Around 1919

## Le Creusot War Memorial

In 1919, Eugène Schneider commissioned Bartholomé for a memorial honoring Le Creusot workers killed in WWI and his son Henri-Paul, who died in aerial combat in 1918. However, "the project was abandoned and in due course another sculptor was found" though Bartholomé had already completed bronze castings of two figures and bas-reliefs now housed at l'Académie François Bourdon.

## Other 1919 War Monuments

**Montbrison War Memorial** (inaugurated May 24, 1920): Featured four soldiers surrounding a bust of Emile Reymond, an aviator and politician killed in 1914, with relief figures representing medicine and aviation.

The Le Creusot memorial represents Bartholomé's only major war monument project from this period that was ultimately completed by another sculptor. His preliminary sculptural elements survive in a public academy rather than as the intended public monument.

## First Sale of Sliced Bread

The first commercial use of the sliced bread machine was by the Chillicothe Baking Company of Chillicothe, Missouri, who sold their first slices on July 7, 1928. Their product, "Kleen Maid Sliced Bread", proved to be a success.

## The Inventor

Otto Frederick Rohwedder of Davenport, Iowa, United States, invented the first single loaf bread-slicing machine. A prototype he built in 1912 was destroyed in a fire, and it was not until 1928 that Rohwedder had a fully working machine ready.

## Early Reception and Growth

Initially, sliced bread faced some skepticism. However, the bread was advertised as "the greatest forward step in the baking industry since bread was wrapped". W.E. Long, who promoted the Holsum Bread brand, used by various independent bakers around the country, pioneered and promoted the packaging of sliced bread, beginning in 1928. In 1930, Wonder Bread, first sold in 1925, started marketing sliced bread nationwide.

This innovation quickly became widespread and fundamentally changed how bread was consumed and prepared in American households.

Alberto Ascari's victory for Ferrari was overshadowed by this accident.

## Birth Date

Sir Frederick Ashton was born September 17, 1904, in Guayaquil, Ecuador.

## Early Career

Ashton studied dancing in London under Léonide Massine, Nicholas Legat, and Marie Rambert, who encouraged his first choreographic efforts, The Tragedy of Fashion (1926) and Capriol Suite (1930). In 1928, he joined Ida Rubinstein's company in Paris, where he also came under the influence of Bronislava Nijinska from whom, he acknowledged, he learned his craft.

Ashton joined the Vic-Wells (later the Sadler's Wells and then the Royal) Ballet in 1933, where he began his long career as both choreographer and dancer.

## Major Choreography List

His major works include such enduring favourites as Façade (1931), Les Rendezvous (1933), Les Patineurs (1937), Symphonic Variations (1946), Illuminations (for the New York City Ballet, 1950), Homage to the Queen (1953), Romeo and Juliet (for the Royal Danish Ballet, 1955), Birthday Offering (1956), Ondine (1958), and La Fille mal gardée (1960). Others included The Dream (1964), a one-act ballet based on Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream; Monotones (Part I, 1965; Part II, 1966), to music of Erik Satie; Jazz Calendar (1968); Enigma Variations (1968); A Month in the Country (1976); and Rhapsody (1981), based on music by Sergey Rachmaninoff.

## Breed Origin and History

The bulldog can be traced back to 13th-century England during the rule of King John. The breed traces its origins to 13th-century England, where they were originally bred for bull-baiting — a brutal blood sport where dogs were pitted against tethered bulls for entertainment. The designation "bull" was applied because of the dog's use in the sport of bull-baiting. This entailed the setting of dogs (after placing wagers on each dog) onto a tethered bull. The dog that grabbed the bull by the nose and pinned it to the ground would be the victor.

Bull-baiting was made illegal in England by the Cruelty to Animals Act 1835. Dedicated breeders saw something beyond the fighting ring — a loyal, courageous companion with an unmistakable personality. Over the following decades, breeders selectively refined the Bulldog's temperament, breeding out aggression and emphasizing gentleness, sociability, and that trademark stubbornness that every Bulldog owner knows and loves.

The founders of the club collected all available information about the breed and its best representatives and developed a new standard for the English Bulldog, which was published on 27 May 1875. The Bulldog was officially recognised by the American Kennel Club in 1886.

## Mascot Use in Schools

English Bulldogs are extremely popular as school and university mascots. In the US alone, the Bulldog represents nearly four dozen universities and 250 secondary schools. English Bulldogs dominate the field – 13 schools use them as mascots.

Some of the better-known Bulldog mascots include the University of Georgia's Uga, Mississippi State's Bully, Georgetown's Jack, Butler's Blue IV, Yale's Handsome Dan, and the United States Marine Corps' Chesty. The history of Handsome Dan dates to 1889, when Andrew Graves '92S, a football player and rower during the days of Walter Camp, first named Yale's mascot.

The Bulldog originated in England and can be traced back to **1210**, when the first official bullbaiting event occurred. The breed was specifically developed for the medieval blood sport of bullbaiting, where dogs fought bulls (or bears) that were tied to stakes.

According to historical records, "the Bulldog can be traced to 1210, the year of the first official bullbaiting in England." These early Bulldogs needed to be exceptionally tough to compete against large bovines.

## Transformation from Fighter to Companion

When bullbaiting was banned in 1835, the breed faced extinction. However, the introduction of formal dog shows in 1859 saved the Bulldog from disappearing. Breeders began selectively breeding for gentler temperaments and different physical characteristics, transforming the fierce fighting dog into the affectionate family companion known today. The breed's modern standards were established between 1859 and 1885, with the first English Bulldog Club formed in 1875.

Based on the search results, here's a comprehensive overview of when the Summer and Winter Olympics were held in the same country in the same year:

## History of Olympics Held in Same Country, Same Year

Between the first Winter Olympics in 1924 and the last ones to be held in the same year as the Summer Olympics in 1992, the Summer and Winter Games took place in the same country three times.

France were the first of only three nations in Olympic history to host both the Summer Games and the Winter Games in the same year, the others being the USA in 1932 and Germany in 1936.

More specifically:
- **1924**: The Summer Olympics were held in Paris, France, and in the same year the inaugural Winter Olympics were held in Chamonix in France.
- **1932**: The Summer Olympics were held in Los Angeles and the Winter Olympics in Lake Placid, both in the USA
- **1936**: The Summer Olympics were held in Berlin and the Winter Olympics in Garmisch-Partenkirchen, both in Germany

## End of the Practice

1936 was the last time the Summer and Winter Olympics were held in the same country in the same year. The last Summer and Winter Games held in the same year were in Barcelona (Summer) and Albertville (Winter) in 1992. In 1986, IOC members decided to alternate the Summer Olympic Games and the Winter Olympic Games on separate four-year cycles in even-numbered years.

## Background

The ship was ordered as the fast luxury passenger liner Izumo Maru by Nippon Yusen Kaisha (Japan Mail Steamship Company) in late 1938, and in exchange for a Navy Ministry subsidy of 60% of her building costs, she was designed to be converted to an aircraft carrier in the event of war.

## Sinking at the Battle of the Philippine Sea

Hiyō was sunk by a gasoline-vapour explosion caused by an American torpedo hit during the Battle of the Philippine Sea on 20 June 1944 with the loss of 247 officers and ratings, about a fifth of her complement. More specifically, the carrier Hiyō was attacked and hit by bombs and aerial torpedoes from four Grumman TBF Avengers from Belleau Wood.

## Historical Significance

The Battle of the Philippine Sea was a major naval battle of World War II on 19–20 June 1944 that eliminated the Imperial Japanese Navy's ability to conduct large-scale carrier actions. The loss of Hiyō was part of a larger Japanese defeat, as the battle concluded with the Japanese losing three carriers and over 400 aircraft, while the U.S. lost 80 planes due to combat and fuel shortages during the return to their carriers.

I've completed the web search on the Avukana Buddha statue and reservoir in Sri Lanka. Here's what I found:

## Overview

The Avukana statue is a standing statue of the Buddha near Kekirawa in North Central Sri Lanka, with a height of more than 14 m (46 ft), depicting the Buddha with a hand raised in reassurance, a variation of the Abhaya mudra.

## Location and Reservoir

The figure is set within a shallow niche and faces east, gazing toward the Kala Wewa reservoir. The Avukana statue faces a large body of water, in this case Kalaveva, an artificial water reservoir complex developed by the Moriya king Dhatusena (r. 455–73 CE) that harnessed water from the Kala Oya river system, allowing agriculture and trade to flourish in the region.

## Construction and Materials

Carved from a large granite rock face, the statue remains partially attached to the rock by a narrow strip left at the back for support. The pedestal on which the Buddha stands takes the form of a lotus flower.

## Dating

There is scholarly debate about when the statue was created. The Avukana statue is widely believed to have been constructed in the 5th century, but Diran K. Dohanian concluded, based on comparisons with Buddhas elsewhere in Sri Lanka and those produced for the Amaravati school, that the Aukana Buddha belongs to the 8th century. This is confirmed by a donative inscription, found in 1951 on the north wall of the shrine, that is written in Sinhala and dates to the 8th century.

## Artistic Significance

The Avukana statue is one of the best examples of a standing statue built in Sri Lanka.

The immediate cause was the suspicious death of the pro-British Sultan Hamad bin Thuwaini on August 25, 1896, and the subsequent succession of Sultan Khalid bin Barghash. The Battle of the Milvian Bridge took place between the Roman Emperors Constantine I and Maxentius on 28 October AD 312. It takes its name from the Milvian Bridge, an important route over the Tiber.

Constantine won the battle and started on the path that led him to end the Tetrarchy and become the sole ruler of the Roman Empire. Maxentius drowned in the Tiber during the battle; his body was later taken from the river and decapitated, and his head was paraded through the streets of Rome on the day following the battle before being sent to Africa.

The battle also had significant religious implications. According to Christian chroniclers Eusebius of Caesarea and Lactantius, the battle marked the beginning of Constantine's conversion to Christianity.

## End Date of the Civil Wars of the Tetrarchy

The civil wars of the Tetrarchy were a series of conflicts between the co-emperors of the Roman Empire, starting from 306 AD with the usurpation of Maxentius and the defeat of Severus, and ending with the defeat of Licinius at the hands of Constantine I in 324 AD.

## Constantine Becoming Sole Ruler

Constantine won the Battle of Chrysopolis on 18 September 324. Licinius and Martinianus surrendered to Constantine at Nicomedia on the promise their lives would be spared, and thus Constantine became the sole emperor of the Roman Empire, ending the civil wars of the Tetrarchy.

In summary, the Civil Wars of the Tetrarchy ended on **September 18, 324 AD** with Constantine's victory at the Battle of Chrysopolis, which made him the sole ruler of the Roman Empire.

## Popes from 312-324 AD

**Pope Miltiades (311-314 AD)**

Pope Miltiades was the bishop of Rome from 311 to his death on 10 or 11 January 314. It was during his pontificate that Emperor Constantine the Great issued the Edict of Milan (313), giving Christianity legal status within the Roman Empire. The pope also received the palace of Empress Fausta where the Lateran Palace, the papal seat and residence of the papal administration, would be built.

**Pope Sylvester I (314-335 AD)**

By the time the council was convened, Miltiades had died on 10 or 11 January 314. He was succeeded by Sylvester I.

## Important Context

It's worth noting that the chronology of the early popes is heavily disputed. Additionally, in 440 A.D. the Roman Bishop Leo I claimed that the Apostle Peter had been given sole rule over the Church by Christ—and that Peter had been the first Bishop of Rome. Thus, Bishop Leo claimed that as Bishop of Rome, he was the rightful heir to Peter's reign. Through this, Leo created the office of the Pope.

## The Dyatlov Pass Incident - What Happened in 1959

The Dyatlov Pass incident was an event in which nine Soviet ski hikers died in the northern part of the Ural Mountains ridge in the Russian SFSR of the Soviet Union on 1 or 2 February 1959 under undetermined circumstances.

### The Expedition

The experienced trekking group from the Ural Polytechnical Institute, led by Igor Dyatlov, went on a hike of the highest difficulty level at that time, and had established a camp on the eastern slopes of Kholat Syakhl mountain. Early in the journey, Yuri Yudin became ill and returned home, a decision that ultimately saved his life.

### The Event

Overnight, the group cut their way out of their tent with knives and fled the campsite, inadequately dressed for the heavy snowfall, strong winds and extreme cold temperatures as low as −40 °C (−40 °F).

### The Deaths

After the group's bodies were discovered, an investigation by Soviet authorities determined that six of them had died from hypothermia while the other three had been killed by physical trauma. They were in various states of dress and had bizarre injuries, with one appearing to have bitten off part of his own knuckle.

### The Investigation

Officials provided only a vague explanation, stating that the hikers had succumbed to an "unknown compelling force." In 2019, Russian authorities reopened the case and conducted a modern review using contemporary scientific methods. In 2020, investigators announced that an avalanche or an avalanche-like snow slab event was the most likely explanation.

## Overview

On 11 June 1955, a multi-vehicle collision occurred during the 1955 24 Hours of Le Mans in Sarthe, France, resulting in the deaths of an estimated 82 to 84 people. The disaster is the deadliest event in motorsport history, prompting multiple European countries to ban motorsports entirely; Switzerland did not lift its ban until 2022.

## What Happened

The disaster occurred at the Circuit de la Sarthe, when a mid-race collision sent Mercedes driver Pierre Levegh and his car into a spectator arena, causing his car to disintegrate and throwing him onto the racetrack, killing him instantly. Debris from the car and the arena flew into the crowd, killing at least 82 people.

## The Cause

The cause of the crash was later determined to have been due to aggressive braking from Jaguar driver Mike Hawthorn. Preparing for his pit stop, he pulled to the right side of the track in front of Austin-Healey driver Lance Macklin and abruptly braked.

## Aftermath and Legacy

The death of the spectators was blamed on inadequate safety standards for the track design. Over the next year, the Automobile Club de l'Ouest (ACO) set about making extensive track improvements and infrastructure changes at the Circuit de la Sarthe—the pit straight was redesigned and widened to remove the kink just before the start-finish line, and to give room for a deceleration lane.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about the Pruett rule and blue moon definition:

The practice of designating the second full moon in a month as "blue" originated with amateur astronomer James Hugh Pruett in 1946. In the March 1946 issue of Sky & Telescope magazine, Pruett wrote an article titled "Once in a Blue Moon." He either misread the Maine almanac's definition or interpreted the meaning of "blue moon" differently, calling it the second full moon in a month.

It's important to note that this definition was based on a misinterpretation. Pruett was referring to the 1937 Maine Farmer's Almanac, but he inadvertently simplified the definition. He wrote that seven times in 19 years there were 13 full moons in a year, giving 11 months with one full moon each and one with two, which he interpreted as the second full moon in a month being called a Blue Moon.

Today, Pruett's misinterpreted "two full moons in a month rule" is recognized worldwide. However, the original "Maine Almanac" rule — the one promoted by Lafleur and later misinterpreted by Pruett — defines a blue moon as the third full moon of a season with four full moons.

## Three-Body Problem and Lunar Apsides

The motion of the apsides—the apogee and perigee of the Moon—is one of the irregularities in the Moon's orbit around Earth. Because the Moon is attracted to both Earth and the Sun, mathematicians calculating its orbit must confront the three-body problem. The two points rotate around Earth with a period of nine years.

## 18th Century French Mathematicians

The three-body problem was the subject of an intense competition between Euler, Alexis-Claude Clairaut, and d'Alembert in the late 1740s and early 1750s. Leonhard Euler, Alexis Clairaut and Jean-Baptiste d'Alembert competed to develop a theory accounting for solar perturbations to the motion of the Moon around the Earth, with Clairaut providing an explanation of the annual 40° rotation of the lunar perigee which had eluded Newton.

## Navigation Applications

This work was important for marine navigation at a time of exploration, as in the absence of accurate clocks that could function at sea, a lunar table along with the observed position of the Moon was the principal method of estimating the longitude.

## 18th Century French Mathematicians and the Three-Body Problem

During the 18th and 19th centuries, the study of the three-body problem by Euler, Clairaut, and d'Alembert led to more accurate predictions about the motions of the Moon and planets. The three-body problem was the subject of an intense competition between Euler, Alexis-Claude Clairaut, and d'Alembert in the late 1740s and early 1750s.

## The Moon's Apsides

One of the numerous irregularities in the orbit of the Moon around Earth is the motion of the apsides—that is, the apogee, or point at which the Moon is farthest from Earth, and the perigee, at which it is nearest. Those two points rotate around Earth with a period of nine years. Even the great Newton could account for only half of the motion of the apsides.

## Connection to Longitude and Sea Navigation

This was of much practical importance in marine navigation, where lunar tables were necessary to accurately determine longitude at sea. In the absence of accurate clocks that could function at sea, a lunar table along with the observed position of the Moon was the principal method of estimating the longitude.

## Early Use of Fourier Series

Notably, Clairaut's use of Fourier series in the three-body problem (1754) predates their use by Joseph Fourier in the analysis of heat conduction! This is a striking historical fact showing Clairaut's innovative mathematical approach predated Fourier's later famous applications.

## Sextant Development and Testing

In 1757, Captain James Campbell designed the sextant and had it made two years later by the instrument-maker, John Bird. This instrument was developed as an improvement on earlier reflecting instruments.

## Lunar Distance Method and Testing

Timekeepers were tested alongside the lunar-distance method, supported by predictive tables and newly developed double-reflection observing instruments – octants, sextants and circles. More specifically, Tobias Mayer was the first to produce a set of tables of sufficient accuracy for lunar-distances, which were published in 1753.

The results of the sea trials conducted on the Board's behalf by Captain John Campbell were inconclusive. However, timekeepers and sextants were tested and put to use on the circumnavigations of James Cook in the 1760s–1770s.

## Duration of Testing and Use

The lunar distance method and sextant underwent significant development and testing throughout the 1750s-1770s, with the late 18th century through the middle of the 19th century marking when navigators could use the Moon with the sextant as a natural clock in the sky.

## Sextant Invention

The navigational sextant was invented in 1731 by John Hadley. However, the sextant was invented independently by Thomas Godfrey in America and John Hadley in England during the 18th century.

## Development and Refinement

The sextant underwent significant improvements throughout the century:

- The earliest known sextant is dated 1757 and was the work of that great master of hand division, John Bird.

- When Nevil Maskelyne, England's future Astronomer Royal, published his lunar distance method in 1764 the immediate need and popular demand for an instrument with the capability to record celestial angles up to 120 of arc was established.

- Perhaps the greatest boon to the production of the sextant came in the period from 1768 to 1774 during which time Jesse Ramsden was given a patent for his perfected dividing engine.

## Purpose for Navigation

Mariners could accurately measure the latitude they were in (position on a north-south line) by measuring the angle of the sun at noon (in the northern hemisphere) or that of the North Star or Polaris (in the southern hemisphere). Additionally, the sextant was derived from the octant in order to provide for the lunar distance method. With the lunar distance method, mariners could determine their longitude accurately.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about John Harrison's marine chronometer development:

## Development Timeline

John Harrison (1693-1776) invented an accurate marine chronometer after several decades of research and development. He invented his first chronometer in 1735 named H1 (Harrison 1) which took him 5 years to build.

After twenty years spent working on the H1, H2 and H3, each more precise and reliable than its predecessor, in 1759 Harrison presented his now famous H4, which was a major breakthrough. The different models were:

- **H1 (1735)**: His first attempt, a large sea clock that showed promise but needed refinement.
- **H2 (1741)**: An improved version that Harrison never tested at sea due to the outbreak of war.
- **H3 (1757)**: A more compact design that introduced new features to combat the effects of temperature and motion.
- **H4 (1759)**: A breakthrough design resembling a large pocket watch, which ultimately won Harrison the longitude prize.

## Testing and Recognition

The 'sea watch' was put to the practical test of travelling on HMS Deptford from Portsmouth to Jamaica from November 1761 to January 1762. The Board of Longitude was still not satisfied; the watch had lost 5.1 seconds on the voyage, and the board demanded more research and more testing. The Board of Longitude finally approved H4 after it was tested again on HMS Tartar on a voyage to Barbados in March-April 1764.

It would take a further twenty years, the H5 and the intervention of George III for John Harrison to receive the acknowledgement he was due.

## Tobias Mayer's Lunar Tables

Tobias Mayer (1723-1762), a German astronomer, became the first to produce a set of tables of measurements of lunar distances that could be used by sailors at sea to measure longitude in 1753. Compiled from Euler's equations and from his own and Bradley's observations at Greenwich, they were published in 1753.

## The Repeating Circle and John Bird

James Bradley commissioned the London instrument maker John Bird (1709–1776) to make a brass copy of a repeating circle, that had been designed by Mayer. Tobias Mayer's design from 1754 was constructed in 1757 by renowned instrument maker John Bird in 1757 as a reflecting circle with a radius of 16" (around 40 cm).

## Testing and Results

The results of the sea trials conducted on the Board's behalf by Captain John Campbell were inconclusive. However, Bradley concluded that Mayer's tables, alongside a good instrument of this sort could determine a ship's longitude to within 1°.

## Development of the Sextant

Campbell incorporated these along with the best elements of the Quadrant into a new instrument, the marine sextant that he went on to develop with the instrument maker John Bird. Mayer's ideas were trialled on a longer British voyage, an expedition to the Atlantic island of St Helena to observe the transit of Venus across the face of the Sun in 1761.

Jean-Charles de Borda (1733–1799) was a French mathematician who further improved the reflecting circle, which had been originally invented by Tobias Mayer. Borda worked to improve the reflecting circle and the repeating circle (invented by his assistant, Étienne Lenoir).

In 1778, he published his method of reducing Lunar Distances for computing the longitude, still regarded as the best of several similar mathematical procedures for navigation and position-fixing in pre-chronometer days. In 1771, Borda embarked on a transatlantic voyage aimed at finding improved methods of longitude determination and testing a number of marine timekeepers.

The reflecting circle became known by various names, including the "Borda circle," reflecting its association with his improvements to the instrument for navigation purposes.
